front: Define **computer**.
back: A computer is an **electronic device** capable of **taking an input**, **processing data**, **storing information** and **providing an output**.

front: What is the difference between data and information?
back: Data that is input is **raw, unprocessed** information, while information is data that **people understand**.

front: Define **mainframe computer**.
back: A mainframe computer is a computer with **huge processing power and data storage capabilities**, built to handle enormous amounts of data and carry out complex calculations.

front: Give three qualities a mainframe computer is designed to have.
back: A mainframe is designed to be **secure** and **reliable**, and to support **large volumes of simultaneous users**.

front: Define **microprocessor**.
back: A microprocessor is an **integrated circuit (IC)** that contains a **central processing unit (CPU)** and is embedded into devices to execute instructions.

front: Give three home systems that a microprocessor is used to monitor and control.
back: Microprocessors monitor and control **central heating systems**, **security alarm systems** and **home entertainment systems**.

front: Give two reasons why a laptop is typically less powerful than a desktop computer.
back: A laptop has **power constraints due to its size** and is designed with a **focus on extending battery life**.

front:
**True or False?**

A laptop computer is easily upgradable.
back:
**False.**

Laptop components are **integrated for size and efficiency**, so a laptop is **not easily upgradable**, unlike a desktop whose parts can be replaced to increase performance.

front: Give three advantages of a laptop computer.
back: A laptop offers **portability**, so it is easy to carry and use on the go, **flexibility**, giving access to the internet and resources from anywhere, and **multi-functionality** for various tasks.

front: What does a mobile phone use to transmit information between people and devices?
back: A mobile phone transmits information using **radio waves**.

front: Smartphones use subscriber identity module (<u>**      **</u>) cards to link the device to a network carrier.
back: Smartphones use subscriber identity module (**SIM**) cards to link the device to a network carrier.

front: Give three features a specialist phone designed for older users might have.
back: A senior phone typically has **larger buttons**, **easy to read displays**, a **simplified user interface**, **emergency alert buttons** and **hearing aid compatibility**.

front: Define **multifunctional device**.
back: A multifunctional device is a device designed to carry out **a wide range of tasks**, **combining functions** that would usually be separate.

front: Define **convergence**.
back: Convergence is the **merging of technologies** that would usually be separate, and it led to the rise of smartphones.

front: What does a games console use to deliver high quality, smooth gameplay?
back: A games console uses **powerful processors and graphics**, along with **online capability** and **controllers** for interactivity.

front: Name five common features of a digital device.
back: Common features are **portability**, **performance**, **storage**, **user interface**, **connectivity**, **media support**, **energy consumption**, **expansion capability** and **security features**.

front: What does the performance of a digital device describe?
back: Performance describes the device's **processing power and memory (RAM)**.

front: What does the expansion capability of a digital device describe?
back: Expansion capability describes whether **more storage, memory or other features can be added**.

front: Define **user interface**.
back: A user interface is **how the user interacts with the operating system**.

front: Name the four types of user interface.
back: The four types are the **Command Line Interface (CLI)**, the **Graphical User Interface (GUI)**, the **menu** interface and the **natural language interface (NLI)**.

front: How does a user interact with a Command Line Interface?
back: A Command Line Interface requires users to interact with the operating system using **text based commands**, and is more commonly used by **advanced users**.

front: A Graphical User Interface uses visual elements known as windows, icons, menus and pointers (<u>**        **</u>).
back: A Graphical User Interface uses visual elements known as windows, icons, menus and pointers (**WIMP**).

front: What kind of input is a Graphical User Interface optimised for?
back: A GUI is optimised for **mouse and touch gesture input**.

front: How does a menu interface present choices to the user?
back: A menu interface presents **successive menus** with a **single option at each stage**, often using buttons or a keypad.

front: Give three places a menu interface is used.
back: Menu interfaces are used in **chip and pin machines**, **vending machines** and **entertainment streaming services**.

front: How does a natural language interface work?
back: A natural language interface uses **the spoken word** to respond to **spoken or textual inputs** from a user.

front:
**True or False?**

A smartphone has higher performance and greater expansion capability than a desktop computer.
back:
**False.**

A smartphone rates **low** on performance and expansion capability, while a desktop rates **high** on both; the smartphone's advantage is **portability**.

front: How does the connectivity of a desktop compare with that of a smartphone?
back: A desktop offers **multiple ports in a wide variety** (such as USB and HDMI), while a smartphone connects **wirelessly** using Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

front: Define **software**.
back: Software is the set of programs that **control the hardware**; it lives on the computer system but **cannot be physically touched**.

front: Define **application software**.
back: Application software is software **chosen by a user** to help them **carry out a specific task**.

front: Define **system software**.
back: System software is software that is **essential for the operation of a computer system**.

front: How is application software different from system software?
back: Application software carries out tasks for the **user**, while system software carries out tasks for the **machine**.

front: Name four essential services carried out by system software.
back: System software provides **compilers**, **linkers**, **device drivers**, **operating systems** and **utilities**.

front: What is the role of a device driver?
back: A device driver **controls hardware components and peripherals**.

front: Give three common categories of application software.
back: Categories include **word processing**, **spreadsheet**, **database management systems**, **control/measurement**, **video editing**, **graphics editing**, **audio editing** and **computer-aided design (CAD)**.

front: Define **utility software**.
back: Utility software is software designed to help **maintain**, **enhance** and **troubleshoot or repair** a computer system.

front: What does defragmentation software do?
back: Defragmentation software **groups fragmented files back together** in order to **improve access speed**.

front:
**True or False?**

Defragmentation can be used on any type of secondary storage.
back:
**False.**

Defragmentation can only be used on **magnetic storage**.

front: Why does data become fragmented on a hard disk drive over time?
back: Data is added in order, but as files are deleted this **leaves gaps**; as new programs and data are added these gaps get filled, so data becomes **fragmented**.

front: What is the difference between lossy and lossless compression?
back: **Lossy** compression removes data, so the original file **cannot be re-created**, while **lossless** compression orders data more efficiently, so the original file **can be re-created**.

front: Task manager allows users to monitor system <u>**                  **</u> in order to help troubleshoot potential problems.
back: Task manager allows users to monitor system **resources** in order to help troubleshoot potential problems.

front: Define **operating system**.
back: An operating system is software that provides an **interface between the user and the hardware** in a computer system.

front: How does an operating system hide the complexity of the hardware from the user?
back: A user does not need to know **where on secondary storage** data is kept, only that it is saved for when they want it again.

front: Name the two main types of operating system.
back: The two main types are **single user operating systems** and **network operating systems (NOS)**.

front: Name four functions of an operating system.
back: An operating system carries out **memory management**, **resource management**, **security** and **print spooling**.

front: What is memory management?
back: Memory management is the process by which the operating system **allocates main memory (RAM)** between different programs that are **open at the same time**.

front: On what basis does the operating system allocate RAM to programs?
back: RAM is allocated based on **priority and fairness**, so system applications may have a higher priority than user applications.

front: How does processor management let a user run several programs at once?
back: The operating system divides processor time into small chunks (**time slicing**) and **allocates them to different programs**, giving the perception of **multitasking**.

front: The CPU can only execute <u>**      **</u> instruction at a time, but it can execute billions of them in one second.
back: The CPU can only execute **one** instruction at a time, but it can execute billions of them in one second.

front: What does input/output management make possible?
back: It makes **plug-and-play (PnP)** functionality possible, **automatically detecting and configuring** new inputs and outputs without manually installing device drivers.

front: What is file management?
back: File management is the process by which the operating system **creates, organises, manipulates and accesses files and folders** on a computer system.

front: What is security management in an operating system?
back: Security management **enables different users to log onto a computer**, with a system administrator able to allocate different **access rights** for different users.

front: What does print spooling do?
back: The spooler creates a **temporary holding area (a queue)** for the print job, and queuing pages **increases efficiency**.

front:
**True or False?**

A single user operating system allows the interface to be customised for different users.
back:
**False.**

A single user operating system has **no option to customise** the user interface for different users.

front: What are office productivity tools?
back: Office productivity tools are applications designed to enable **common work-related tasks** to be carried out, and are often combined into a single **application suite**.

front: What is word processing software used for?
back: Word processing software is used primarily for tasks involving **text and images**, such as letters, reports, essays and books.

front: What is spreadsheet software used for?
back: Spreadsheet software is used for tasks involving **calculations**, allowing users to **model financial situations** and answer **'what if'** questions.

front: What is desktop publishing software used for?
back: Desktop publishing software is used for tasks that involve **complicated page layouts**, such as newsletters and leaflets.

front: Name three common features of database software.
back: Database software offers **data entry form design**, **queries** to select data meeting a certain criteria, and **reports** to display data in a readable format.

front: Define **web authoring software**.
back: Web authoring software is software designed to allow the **creation of websites**.

front: Websites are written in <u>**        **</u> and translated by web browsers so that users can see and read them.
back: Websites are written in **HTML** and translated by web browsers so that users can see and read them.

front: What type of interface does web authoring software use?
back: It uses a **What You See Is What You Get (WYSIWYG)** interface, which helps users with little or no HTML experience to create web pages.

front: What does image editing software allow users to do?
back: Image editing software allows users to **manipulate and enhance digital photographs and images**.

front: Name three common features of image editing software.
back: Features include **resizing**, **adjusting brightness and contrast**, **applying filters**, **red-eye removal** and **cropping**.

front: Name three common features of sound editing software.
back: Features include **cutting and joining audio clips**, **altering volume**, **changing tempo**, **adding effects** and **applying audio processing**.

front: What is presentation software designed to do?
back: Presentation software allows users to create **multimedia content** that is typically displayed on **slides**.

front: Name three common features of presentation software.
back: Features include **transitions and animations**, **presenter notes**, and **automatic or timed navigation**.

front: Define **control software**.
back: Control software uses **sensors to capture inputs**, processes them and produces an output that makes something happen in the **physical environment**.

front: Give two devices that control software can send output commands to.
back: Control software can send commands to **actuators** and **motors**.

front:
**True or False?**

The critical path shows the longest time a project will take to complete.
back:
**False.**

The critical path allows a project manager to see the **shortest** time a project will take to complete.

front: Define **project management software**.
back: Project management software is designed to make the **organisation of projects** more efficient by **tracking individual tasks**.

front: What is a milestone in project management software?
back: A milestone is a **time or date by which a task must be completed**.

front: What does a timeline show in project management software?
back: A timeline shows a **graphical representation of events** and the **time and order** in which they occur; **Gantt charts** are often used to visualise project timelines.

front: Define **software licence**.
back: A software licence is a **legal agreement** that lays out the rules for **how software can and cannot be used**.

front: Name the two main types of software licence.
back: The two main types are **free or open source** and **proprietary**.

front: The two types of software licence have very different rules on usage, <u>**                    **</u> and support.
back: The two types of software licence have very different rules on usage, **distribution** and support.

front:
**True or False?**

In the term 'free software', 'free' refers to the cost of the software.
back:
**False.**

'Free' means **free from restrictions**, not free of cost, and an answer based on cost is **not accepted**.

front: What does open source software give users access to?
back: Open source software gives users access to the **source code**, which they can **edit, change and distribute**.

front: Give two features of proprietary software.
back: Proprietary software **costs money**, is produced by **professional companies**, and receives **more regular official updates, support, upgrades and fixes**.

front: Give two advantages of free or open source software.
back: It **allows collaboration** with others who want the same modifications, **less buggy versions may appear faster**, it is **usually free** so suits limited budgets, and it generally has **strong social support**.

front: Give two disadvantages of free or open source software.
back: It **relies on the support of other users**, **expert knowledge** is needed to edit the code, it **may not receive regular updates**, and it could be **more open to exploitation** through users adding malicious code.

front: Give two advantages of proprietary software.
back: It offers **generally free customer support**, it is **created to professional standards**, and there is **always someone to go back to** with any problems.

front: Give two disadvantages of proprietary software.
back: The **cost can be significant**, **expansion is limited** to what is available, it **relies on one company**, and it **may not fully meet the needs** of the user.

front: Define **communication software**.
back: Communication software is software that provides **remote access to systems**, so that files and messages in text, image, audio or video format can be **exchanged between different computers or users**.

front: Name four types of communication software.
back: Common types are **web browsers**, **email**, **social media**, **SMS/MMS** and **instant messaging**.

front: What is the purpose of a web browser?
back: The purpose of a web browser is to **render hypertext markup language (HTML)** and **display web pages**.

front: How does a web browser turn HTML into something a user can read?
back: It **interprets the code** in HTML documents and **translates it into a visual display** for the user.

front: Name three main uses of email.
back: The main uses of email are **personal communication**, **professional correspondence** and **marketing**.

front: Name three things a company's acceptable use guidelines for email usually cover.
back: Guidelines usually cover the **purpose** of the email, using **acceptable language**, and email **security**, including anti-virus software.

front: What do SMS and MMS stand for?
back: SMS stands for **short messaging service** and MMS stands for **multimedia messaging service**.

front: SMS allows a maximum of <u>**      **</u> text characters per message.
back: SMS allows a maximum of **160** text characters per message.

front:
**True or False?**

An internet connection is required to send an SMS message.
back:
**False.**

SMS and MMS use a **mobile phone network**, so **no internet connection** is required.

front: What can an MMS message include that an SMS message cannot?
back: MMS allows **more than 160 characters** and can include **video, animations, images and audio**.

front: What does instant messaging require in order to work?
back: Instant messaging requires an **internet connection** to allow multimedia communication between single users and groups of users.

front: Name two extra features offered by instant messaging.
back: Instant messaging can show **when users are typing (online/offline status)** and can **include location data**.

front: What do privacy settings on a social media platform allow a user to do?
back: Privacy settings allow users to **control who can see their content**.

front: Give three reasons why software is updated.
back: Software is updated to **fix bugs or software vulnerabilities**, **increase compatibility with newer operating systems**, **improve performance**, **introduce new features** and **improve usability**.

front: How are software updates usually obtained?
back: Updates are typically **downloaded from the internet**, either by the user or **automatically from within the software** itself.

front: What two steps does a user take to update a piece of software?
back: The user **downloads** the update file and then **installs** it.

front: Why can an operating system schedule updates?
back: Scheduling allows updates to **suit user needs** and **minimise disruption**.

front: Software updates typically require the removal of components, to be replaced with <u>**      **</u> ones.
back: Software updates typically require the removal of components, to be replaced with **new** ones.

front: Name three risks of updating software.
back: The risks are **incompatibility** with older hardware or software, **workflow disruption** while users adjust to new features or interface changes, and **update issues** where the installation goes wrong and causes data loss.

front: Why do flaws in newly released software matter?
back: Software is often released in a **less than perfect state**, and any flaws or vulnerabilities provide an **opportunity for hackers**.

front:
**True or False?**

Choosing not to update software carries no security consequences.
back:
**False.**

Unpatched or outdated software can lead to **data breaches** and the **installation of malware**.

front: What does a corrective update do?
back: A corrective update **fixes or patches bugs**.

front: What does an adaptive update do?
back: An adaptive update **improves compatibility**, for example with operating system or hardware changes.

front: What does a perfective update do?
back: A perfective update **adds new features**.

front: What does a preventative update do?
back: A preventative update **protects against new security vulnerabilities**.

front: Why might an update cause software to stop working on an older machine?
back: An update **replaces components**, and the new components **may not work with older hardware or software**.

front: Define **input device**.
back: An input device is a **hardware component** that allows users to **input data or commands into the system**, which the computer then processes to produce an output.

front: What does OMR stand for, and what does it read?
back: OMR stands for **Optical Mark Recognition**, and it reads **marks made in pen or pencil**, for example on an exam paper.

front: What does OCR stand for, and what does it do?
back: OCR stands for **Optical Character Recognition**, and it converts **text into digital data**.

front:
**True or False?**

Optical Mark Recognition can read handwriting.
back:
**False.**

OMR is **limited to specific forms** and **cannot read handwriting**; the form must also be completed accurately.

front: How does a resistive touchscreen register a touch?
back: **Pressure** causes the **layers to 'touch'**, and this type of screen is **durable**.

front: How does a capacitive touchscreen register a touch?
back: The screen **conducts electricity**, so a finger causes a **change in electrical charge** that can be **measured precisely**.

front: Give two disadvantages of a barcode scanner.
back: A barcode scanner **requires line-of-sight**, barcodes are **easily damaged**, and barcodes can be **swapped or altered by consumers**.

front: What does a biometric scanner recognise?
back: A biometric scanner uses **fingerprint, facial, voice or iris recognition**.

front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of an RFID reader for contactless payments.
back: RFID gives a **fast transaction with no PIN** and transfers data wirelessly and securely, but the **transaction limit is smaller** and **RFID signals can be read or intercepted**.

front: Data from an analogue sensor must be converted to digital data using an <u>**      **</u>.
back: Data from an analogue sensor must be converted to digital data using an **ADC**.

front: Give one advantage of using sensors to collect data.
back: Sensors are generally **accurate**, provide **real-time information**, work **automatically**, and can collect data from places where there may be **a threat to human life**.

front: Define **output device**.
back: An output device is a **hardware component** that **receives information from a computer system** and **presents it to the user** in a comprehensible form.

front: How are the screen size and the resolution of a monitor each measured?
back: **Screen size** is measured **diagonally in inches**, while **resolution** is the **number of pixels measured horizontally** across the screen.

front: What is the key difference between how a laser printer and an inkjet printer put an image on paper?
back: A laser printer uses electronically charged **toner**, which is **dry ink**, while an inkjet printer sprays tiny dots of **wet ink** separated into black, cyan, magenta and yellow.

front: How does a dot matrix printer put ink on paper, and when is it useful?
back: Paper is **impacted through a ribbon** of ink, which makes it useful when printing **multiple copies** or multi-part forms.

front: Name two peripheral devices that could be used to input text by people who cannot use a mouse and keyboard.
back: Options include a **microphone**, a **touchscreen**, a **trackpad**, a **graphics tablet**, and a **camera, eye tracker or gesture reader**.

front: Define **storage device**.
back: A storage device is the **hardware that reads from and writes to** different storage media, providing **non-volatile secondary storage** that retains digital data within a computer system.

front: Name the three types of storage device.
back: The three types are **magnetic**, **solid state** and **optical**.

front: How does magnetic storage represent binary 0s and 1s?
back: Magnetic storage uses **magnets (polarity)** to store binary 0s and 1s.

front: How does solid state storage represent binary 0s and 1s?
back: Solid state storage uses **electronic circuits** to store binary 0s and 1s.

front: How does optical storage represent binary 0s and 1s?
back: Optical storage uses **lasers** to burn the surface of a disk, creating **pits and lands** suitable for storing binary 0s and 1s.

front: Give two advantages of magnetic storage.
back: Magnetic storage offers **high capacity** and a **low cost per gigabyte**, with **moderate read/write speed**.

front: Give three disadvantages of magnetic storage.
back: Magnetic storage has poor **durability** because moving parts can be damaged if dropped, poor **portability** because it is heavy and bulky, poor **reliability** because it is prone to mechanical failure, and it is **noisy** because the disks spin.

front: Give two disadvantages of solid state storage.
back: Solid state storage has a **very high cost per gigabyte** and **limited read/write cycles**.

front:
**True or False?**

Optical storage has a very high capacity and very fast read/write access.
back:
**False.**

Optical storage has **very low capacity** and **very slow read/write access**; its advantage is a **very low cost per gigabyte**.

front: Why is solid state storage a good choice for a smartphone?
back: Solid state storage has **no moving parts**, so there is **less risk of damage from movement**, it **takes up less space** and it **uses less power**, giving longer battery life.

front: Define **capacity of storage**.
back: Capacity of storage describes the **amount of binary digits** that can be stored on a digital device.

front: How many bits are in a nibble, and how many are in a byte?
back: A nibble is **4 bits** and a byte is **8 bits**.

front: 1 kibibyte (KiB) is <u>**          **</u> bytes, because binary prefixes work to the power of 2.
back: 1 kibibyte (KiB) is **1024** bytes, because binary prefixes work to the power of 2.

front: What is the difference between a kibibyte and a kilobyte?
back: A **kibibyte** uses **binary prefixes** and is 1024, while a **kilobyte** uses **decimal prefixes** and is 1000.

front: Define **storage media**.
back: Storage media is the **physical media that holds non-volatile data**.

front: How does a storage device interact with its storage media?
back: Each storage device has a **specific read/write mechanism built in** to interact with a particular storage media, so magnetic tape media is read by a magnetic storage device.

front: What is a hard disk made up of?
back: A hard disk is made up of **platters** that spin on a **central spindle**, with a **read/write head** that moves on an arm across the platter.

front: What two things influence how long a hard disk takes to read or write data?
back: The time taken depends on **how fast the platters spin**, measured in revolutions per minute (RPM), and **how fast the head moves** across the platter.

front: Give three uses of hard disks.
back: Hard disks are used in **personal computers**, **servers** and **backups**.

front: What is the difference between recordable and re-writable optical media?
back: **All** optical media is **recordable** (CD-R, DVD-R, BD-R), but only **some** can be **re-written** (CD-RW, DVD-RW, BD-RE).

front: A CD holds up to <u>**            **</u> of data.
back: A CD holds up to **700 MB** of data.

front: How much data does a single sided, single layer DVD hold?
back: A single sided, single layer DVD holds **4.7 GB**, rising to **18 GB** for double sided, double layer.

front: How much data does a single sided Blu-ray disc hold?
back: A single sided Blu-ray holds **25 GB**, and a double sided one holds **50 GB**.

front: Why is flash media more reliable than a hard disk?
back: Flash media contains **no moving parts**, and it also has **very fast read/write speeds**.

front:
**True or False?**

Magnetic tape has very fast read/write speeds.
back:
**False.**

Magnetic tape has **very slow read/write speeds**, which is why it is used for **whole system backups and archives** rather than everyday access.

front: What is magnetic tape now used for?
back: Magnetic tape is **old technology** originally used for recording sound, and is now used to **store vast amounts of data** for **whole system backups and archives**.

Define **RAM**.
back: RAM (Random Access Memory) is **primary storage** that is directly connected to the CPU and holds the **data and instructions currently in use**.

front: What does it mean to say that RAM is volatile?
back: It means the **contents of RAM are lost when the power is turned off**.

front: How do data and instructions get into RAM for the CPU to use?
back: They must be **copied from secondary storage**.

front: Why can adding more RAM improve a computer's performance?
back: RAM capacity **can be increased**, and more RAM means **more programs can be open at the same time** without relying on slower secondary storage.

front: Define **ROM**.
back: ROM (Read Only Memory) is **primary storage** that holds the **first instructions a computer needs to start up**, known as the boot file.

front: ROM contains the <u>**            **</u>, which stands for Basic Input Output System.
back: ROM contains the **BIOS**, which stands for Basic Input Output System.

front: Where is ROM located in a computer system?
back: ROM is a small **memory chip** located on the computer's **motherboard**.

front: How does the speed of ROM compare with RAM and secondary storage?
back: ROM is **much faster than secondary storage** but **slower than RAM**.

front:
**True or False?**

The contents of ROM are lost when the power is turned off.
back:
**False.**

ROM is **non-volatile**, so its contents are **not lost** when the power is turned off.

front: Give three differences between RAM and ROM.
back: RAM stores **data and programs in use** while ROM stores the **boot file**; RAM capacity is **variable** while ROM is **fixed**; RAM contents are **temporary** while ROM contents are **permanent**; RAM is **read and write** while ROM is **read only**; RAM is **volatile** while ROM is **non-volatile**.

front: What do EPROM and EEPROM stand for?
back: EPROM is **erasable programmable read only memory** and EEPROM is **electronically erasable programmable read only memory**.

front: Define **flash memory**.
back: Flash memory is **a type of EEPROM** that is **non-volatile**, with **fast access times** and **low power consumption**.

front: Give three places flash memory is used.
back: Flash memory is used in **solid state drives**, **USB drives** and **SD memory cards**.

front: Why does reducing the amount of RAM slow a computer down?
back: Programs become **more reliant on being read from secondary storage or virtual memory**, which has **slower read/write times than RAM**.

front: What is the purpose of the CPU?
back: The purpose of the Central Processing Unit is to **execute instructions**, which it achieves by completing **processor cycles**.

front: Name the three stages of the processor cycle.
back: The three stages are **fetch**, **decode** and **execute**.

front: What happens during the fetch stage of the processor cycle?
back: The next instruction or data is **fetched from the computer's memory (RAM)** and brought back to the CPU.

front: What happens during the decode stage of the processor cycle?
back: The CPU **works out what is required** from the instruction.

front: Give two things the CPU might do during the execute stage.
back: The CPU **carries out the instruction**, which could mean **performing a calculation**, **storing a result back in main memory**, or **fetching data from a different location** in main memory.

front: Define **clock speed**.
back: Clock speed is the measure of a processor's speed, giving the **number of processor cycles that can take place in 1 second**.

front: Clock speed is measured in <u>**            **</u> (Hz).
back: Clock speed is measured in **Hertz** (Hz).

front: How many instructions per second can a clock speed of 3.5 GHz perform?
back: A clock speed of 3.5 GHz can perform up to **3.5 billion instructions per second**, because a gigahertz means a billion cycles per second.

front: What is a core?
back: A core **works like it is its own CPU**, so a multi-core processor has **multiple separate processing units** that can fetch, decode and execute instructions at the same time.

front: How many instructions per second can a quad-core CPU running at 3 GHz perform?
back: 4 cores × 3 GHz gives **12 billion instructions per second**.

front:
**True or False?**

A slower clock speed allows more instructions to be fetched and executed per second.
back:
**False.**

The **faster** the clock speed, the **more instructions** can be fetched and executed per second.

front: How does a faster processor improve a user's experience when playing a game?
back: A faster processor **fetches, decodes and executes more instructions per second**, so **graphics render more quickly and at greater resolution**, making the visuals **smoother** and the environment **more realistic**, and allowing **more actions** to be carried out.

front: What must be considered when selecting digital devices and peripherals for a user?
back: It is crucial to consider the **tasks they are intended for** and the **user's requirements**.

front: Why might a desktop be chosen over a tablet for graphic design and video editing?
back: A desktop is ideal for **high-performance tasks**, whereas a tablet is lightweight and better suited to **reading, browsing and simple applications**.

front: What is an ergonomic keyboard designed to do?
back: An ergonomic keyboard is designed to **reduce strain on the hands, wrists and arms**, preventing **repetitive stress injuries (RSI)**.

front: How does a screen reader help a visually impaired user?
back: A screen reader **reads on-screen text aloud** to the user.

front: What is the difference between a Braille display and a Braille printer?
back: A **Braille display** enables visually impaired users to **read digital text**, while a **Braille printer** prints a **hard copy** of a document in Braille.

front: A <u>**              **</u> pen allows users with dyslexia to interpret text.
back: A **reading** pen allows users with dyslexia to interpret text.

front: How does a haptic feedback device help a user?
back: It **provides feedback to the user without reliance on visuals or sound**.

front: Name the three categories software can be broken into when matching it to a user's needs.
back: The three categories are **productivity software**, **specialised software** and **accessibility software**.

front: Give three examples of specialised software.
back: Specialised software includes **CAD programs** for design and engineering, **graphic design tools** for creating visual content, and **database management systems** for organising large data sets.

front: What does voice recognition software allow a user to do?
back: It allows users to **control devices and input text using voice commands**.

front: Give three display or audio settings that can be adjusted to suit a user's needs.
back: **Display settings** such as screen resolution, brightness and font size can be adjusted, along with **audio settings** such as volume and output options, and **accessibility features** such as high-contrast modes, screen magnifiers and voice commands.

front: Name three ways hardware and software can be configured to meet a user's needs.
back: Through **network settings**, **user permissions** and **security protocols**.

front: What does setting user permissions on a system achieve?
back: It **assigns user roles**, **restricts access to sensitive data** and **ensures data security**.

front:
**True or False?**

A gesture interface is intended for users with high levels of manual dexterity.
back:
**False.**

A gesture interface allows data entry for those with **low levels of mobility or dexterity**.

front: What does satellite communication use to carry signals?
back: Satellite communication uses **radio waves**, sent between **satellites** and **ground stations** on earth.

front: Give one advantage and two disadvantages of satellite communication.
back: The service is **always available**, but it can be **interrupted by weather conditions** and its signals **do not pass through solid objects**.

front: How does a television picture reach a home by satellite?
back: A video signal is **sent from a broadcaster to a satellite**, then back to earth to an **antenna connected to a set-top box** or directly to a television, which **decodes the signal**.

front: <u>**          **</u> is the international standard for broadcasting digital television.
back: **DVB** is the international standard for broadcasting digital television.

front: What do DVB-T and DAB stand for?
back: DVB-T is **Digital Video Broadcasting Terrestrial** and DAB is **Digital Audio Broadcasting**.

front:
**True or False?**

The transmitters used for digital television and radio are carried on satellites.
back:
**False.**

The transmitters used for DVB-T and DAB are **based on earth**; it is satellite broadcasting that uses orbiting satellites.

front: Give two advantages of digital television and radio.
back: Digital broadcasting gives **improved video and audio quality** and **access to more channels or stations**.

front: What is HDMI used to carry?
back: High Definition Multimedia Interface carries **high definition video and audio signals**.

front: What is a mini-jack used for?
back: A mini-jack is a **3.5 mm** connector commonly used to connect **headphones, speakers and microphones** to devices.

front: What is Ethernet, and what is USB used for?
back: **Ethernet** is the networking standard for connecting devices to a **local area network (LAN)**, while **USB** connects and powers various devices such as printers, flash drives, keyboards and mice.

front: Give two advantages of using a wired method to connect to a smartphone.
back: A wired connection is **faster, with higher bandwidth and lower latency**, gives a **more stable connection**, suffers **less interference**, is **more secure**, and needs **no password**.

front: Give two advantages of using a wireless method to connect to a smartphone.
back: The user **can move around while transferring data**, does not have to **waste time finding and connecting cables**, avoids the **cost of cables**, and there are **no trailing wires** to create a hazard.

front: Name five wireless methods of communication.
back: **Wi-Fi** connects devices to a LAN, **Bluetooth** connects two devices over very short distances, **infra-red (IR)** transmits tiny amounts of data over very short distances, **NFC** uses close proximity RFID, and **4G and 5G** provide internet access to mobile devices.

front: Define **local area network (LAN)**.
back: A local area network is a network covering a **small geographical area** (under 1 mile), where **all of the hardware is owned by the company, organisation or household using it**.

front: Name three types of connection a LAN uses.
back: A LAN uses **unshielded twisted pair (UTP) cable**, **fibre optic cable** or **wireless connections (Wi-Fi)**.

front: Give three advantages of a LAN.
back: A LAN allows **centralised management** of updates, backups and software installations, lets devices be **secured** with firewalls and antivirus software, lets users **share resources** such as printers, and lets users **collaborate and share files and folders**.

front: Give three disadvantages of a LAN.
back: If **hardware fails** the network may not function, networks are **more prone to attacks** than standalone computers, access can be **slow depending on network traffic**, and they **require maintenance** which can be costly.

front: Define **wide area network (WAN)**.
back: A wide area network is a network covering a **large geographical area** (over 1 mile), made up of a **collection of LANs joined together**.

front: What device connects the computers on a WAN?
back: The computers on a WAN are connected via **routers**.

front:
**True or False?**

All the hardware used to connect a WAN is owned by the organisation using it.
back:
**False.**

On a WAN the connecting hardware is **not all owned** by the organisation using it — telephone lines, for example, are owned by telecommunication companies. On a **LAN**, all the hardware is owned by the user.

front: Name three things a WAN uses to connect its LANs together.
back: A WAN uses **fibre optic cable**, **telephone lines** and **satellite**.

front: Define **personal area network (PAN)**.
back: A personal area network is a network used for the **transmission of data between devices in close proximity**, with a **very short range** of about 10 metres.

front: <u>**                **</u> is the most widely used personal area network.
back: **Bluetooth** is the most widely used personal area network.

front: Give three devices that typically make use of a PAN.
back: Typical devices are **wireless headphones**, **mobile phones**, **tablets** and **laptops**.

front: Define **tethering**.
back: Tethering is when a **host device shares its internet connection** with other connected devices.

front: Give two things that can limit a user's ability to tether.
back: Tethering can be **enabled or disabled as part of the mobile contract**, and some network providers **charge extra** to use the feature.

front: What does a device communicate with when using Wi-Fi?
back: Devices communicate with a **hotspot** or a **wireless access point (WAP)**, which can be a standalone device or built into a router or switch.

front: Give three situations where Wi-Fi is preferred over Bluetooth.
back: Wi-Fi is preferred when **high speed data transfer** is required, when **long range communication** is required, and when **many devices need to be connected at the same time**.

front: Give three advantages of Wi-Fi.
back: Wi-Fi offers **portability**, since location is only limited by range, low **cost** to set up and add devices, and good **compatibility**, since most devices have a built-in Wi-Fi adapter.

front: Give three disadvantages of Wi-Fi.
back: Wi-Fi has **slower data transfer than Ethernet**, is **less secure than Ethernet**, and **relies on signal strength to the WAP**, so signals can be obstructed.

front: What is Bluetooth typically used for?
back: Bluetooth is typically used for a **direct connection between two devices**, such as headphones, controllers, keyboards and mice.

front: What happens when two devices pair over Bluetooth?
back: They **exchange a cryptographic key**, which is used to generate a **secret shared key** that **encrypts the data** between them, creating a **Wireless Personal Area Network (WPAN)**.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of Bluetooth.
back: Bluetooth is **ideal for personal devices and ad-hoc connections** and has **very low power consumption**, but it has **very slow transfer speeds**, data **can be intercepted by anyone in range**, and it has a **short range**.

front: Bluetooth has a maximum range of about <u>**            **</u> metres, while Wi-Fi reaches about 100 metres.
back: Bluetooth has a maximum range of about **30** metres, while Wi-Fi reaches about 100 metres.

front: How many devices can connect over Bluetooth compared with Wi-Fi?
back: Bluetooth supports a maximum of **7** connections, while Wi-Fi supports up to **30**.

front: Define **GPS**.
back: Global Positioning System is a **satellite system used to track the exact location of an object**, using orbiting satellites to receive, amplify and transmit signals.

front:
**True or False?**

GPS works reliably without a direct line of sight.
back:
**False.**

GPS **requires a direct line of sight**, and its signal can suffer **interference due to weather or obstacles**.

front: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of GPS.
back: GPS offers a **wide coverage area**, **real-time data transmission**, improved communication in **remote locations** and **accurate location tracking**, but it has **expensive setup and maintenance**, **signal interference**, **limited bandwidth** and raises **privacy concerns**.

front: What do 3G and 4G refer to, and how do they differ?
back: They are the **3rd and 4th generations of mobile data networks**, giving mobile devices wireless access to the internet; each generation has a **faster transfer rate** and **improved capacity for more users**.

front: What is infra-red used for?
back: Infra-red transfers **very small amounts of data** to a device in **direct line of sight**, and is commonly used in remotes to control televisions, audio receivers and home entertainment equipment.

front: Give two things that can disrupt an infra-red signal.
back: Infra-red uses **light waves**, so **walls or obstacles can block the signal** and **sunlight can affect it**.

front: What is the difference between passive and active NFC?
back: **Passive** NFC uses **energy from the reader**, while **active** NFC **has its own power source** — smartphones use active NFC for contactless payments.

front: Define **bandwidth**.
back: Bandwidth is the **amount of data that can be carried by a connection in one second**, measured in **bits per second**.

front: Define **latency**.
back: Latency is the **delay between data being sent and received**.

front: Give three things a higher bandwidth can improve.
back: Higher bandwidth improves **upload and download speeds**, **online gaming** and **streaming high definition video**.

front: Define **buffer**.
back: A buffer is a **temporary area of memory** holding enough downloaded data to play a few seconds of streamed content.

front: What condition must be met for content to stream successfully?
back: Data must be downloaded to the buffer **at a faster rate than it is being emptied**, otherwise the buffer empties and **playback will pause**.

front: Why does a large delay between data being sent and received increase the error rate?
back: A big delay means **more data will be on the network causing collisions**, which leads to **even more packets being sent** as the error rate increases.

front: How does high latency affect a user playing a fast paced online game?
back: High latency causes **lag**, so the game does **not respond as quickly** to the user's commands, putting them at a disadvantage against players with lower latency.

front: How does high latency affect a video call?
back: It **increases the time it takes for data to be transferred between devices**, so voice and video become **out of sync, lagging or delayed**.

front: Name four factors that affect the speed and volume of data transfer.
back: **Interference**, the **transfer method**, **blockages** and **distance**.

front: Why does distance reduce the speed of a data transfer?
back: The **strength of both wired and wireless signals reduces** as data has to travel further, so **more packets have to be requested again**.

front:
**True or False?**

A wireless connection can carry more frequencies than a wired one, giving it a higher bandwidth.
back:
**False.**

**Wired** connections can carry more frequencies, so they have a **higher bandwidth** than wireless connections.

front: Compare wired and wireless connections on security and portability.
back: Wired has **better physical security** but its location is **limited by the physical cable**, while wireless is **less secure and easier to intercept** but its location is **only limited by range**.

front: Fibre optic is a type of cable that uses <u>**            **</u> to transmit data on a wide area network.
back: Fibre optic is a type of cable that uses **light** to transmit data on a wide area network.

front: Give three advantages of fibre optic over copper cable.
back: Fibre transmits data at a **much higher speed** with a **much higher bandwidth**, **does not suffer from interference** so is the most secure option for sensitive data, and can **cover long distances without degradation**.

front: Give two drawbacks of copper cable.
back: Copper **degrades over time**, which limits its range, and it **suffers from interference**, which can disrupt data quality; it is also **slower with lower bandwidth** than fibre.

front: Define **IP address**.
back: An IP (Internet Protocol) address is a **unique identifier** given to devices which communicate over the **internet (WAN)**, making it possible to **deliver data to the right device**.

front: How is an IP address allocated to a device?
back: It can be allocated **by a network administrator** or assigned **dynamically by a DHCP server**.

front: How is an IPv4 address written?
back: IPv4 is written as **4 blocks of denary numbers between 0 and 255**, separated by **full stops**, with each block one byte and each address 4 bytes.

front: How is an IPv6 address written?
back: IPv6 is written as **8 blocks of 4 hexadecimal digits**, separated by **colons**, with each block 2 bytes and each address 16 bytes.

front: Why was IPv6 needed?
back: IPv4 provides just over **4 billion unique addresses**, which is not enough for over **7 billion people** with countless devices each.

front: Define **MAC address**.
back: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a **universally unique identifier** given to devices which communicate over a **local area network (LAN)**.

front: When is a MAC address assigned to a device?
back: Any device containing a **Network Interface Card (NIC)** has a MAC address **assigned during manufacturing**.

front: How is a MAC address written, and what do its parts mean?
back: A MAC address is **12 hexadecimal digits** grouped in pairs; the **first three pairs are the manufacturer ID number (OUI)** and the **last three pairs are the serial number** of the network interface card.

front: Give three uses of a MAC address.
back: MAC addresses can **restrict or allow access to a network**, **identify a device** on a network, **track a device**, and **assign static or fixed IP addresses**.

front: MAC addresses make it possible for <u>**            **</u> to efficiently forward data to the intended recipient.
back: MAC addresses make it possible for **switches** to efficiently forward data to the intended recipient.

front: Describe two differences between IP addresses and MAC addresses.
back: An IP address is **dynamic and can change** while a MAC address is **static and cannot change**; an IP address is used to communicate on a **WAN or the internet** while a MAC address is used on a **LAN**.

front:
**True or False?**

When a device moves to a different network, its MAC address changes.
back:
**False.**

The **MAC address stays the same** when a device moves network; it is the **IP address** that changes.

front: Define **device name**.
back: A device name is a way for users to **describe or name a device** so that it is **easier to identify on a network**.

front: Why are device names not used by devices to communicate?
back: Device names are **not always unique**; they are **set by users** in the device's operating system or from a router.

front: Name the two most common types of cable in a wired network.
back: The two most common are **Ethernet** and **fibre optic**.

front: What does Ethernet cable carry, and over what kind of network?
back: Ethernet is a wired networking standard that carries **electrical signals** between devices on a **local area network (LAN)**.

front: Ethernet uses <u>**                    **</u> cables (CAT5) to allow duplex communication.
back: Ethernet uses **twisted pair** cables (CAT5) to allow duplex communication.

front: Why is fibre optic the most secure option for sending sensitive data?
back: Fibre optic cable **does not suffer from interference**, and it also carries data at much higher speed and bandwidth over long distances without degradation.

front: What does a wireless access point do?
back: A wireless access point (WAP) **allows wireless devices to connect to a local area network**, connecting to a switch or hub via an Ethernet cable.

front: Why might a building need more than one wireless access point?
back: The **range of a WAP is limited**, so multiple access points are used to give complete coverage of a home or business.

front: State three tasks carried out by a router.
back: A router **receives packets**, **forwards packets**, **maintains a routing table**, **identifies the most efficient path** to the destination, and **assigns IP addresses** to devices.

front: Define **gateway**.
back: A gateway is a device that **bridges the connection between two different types of network**, translating between different network protocols.

front: What does a switch do, and why is it called an active device?
back: A switch **allows multiple wired devices to connect to a LAN**, and it is **active** because it can **inspect network data and route it to the correct device**, reducing traffic on the network.

front: What does a booster do?
back: A booster **amplifies a network signal** in order to **extend the normal range**, and can be used with both wired and wireless networks.

front:
**True or False?**

A wireless access point can never act as a booster.
back:
**False.**

A wireless access point **can be configured to act as a booster**, in what is known as **repeater mode**.

front: Define **server**.
back: A server is a **dedicated computer that shares its resources** with the devices that connect to it, which are known as **clients**.

front: Name five common types of server.
back: **File**, **web**, **print**, **authentication** and **application** servers.

front: What does an authentication server do?
back: It **stores usernames and passwords** that can be checked when a user logs in, and authenticated users receive a **certificate** that allows access to resources.

front: What does a print server do?
back: A print server **manages print jobs** and **organises the queue** so that individual printers are not overloaded.

front: Define **web browser**.
back: A web browser is a software application used to **locate, retrieve and display content** on the **World Wide Web**.

front: Name four common features of a web browser.
back: A **home page**, the ability to **bookmark favourites**, a **history of visited websites**, and **hyperlinks** that allow users to navigate between pages.

front: Define **Internet Service Provider (ISP)**.
back: An Internet Service Provider is a **company that provides access to the internet** to users and businesses.

front: How does an ISP provide internet access, and how is it paid for?
back: The ISP **leases equipment and telecommunication lines** to users, and generally **charges a subscription fee**.

front: Define **search engine**.
back: A search engine is a tool that **locates and displays web pages related to the search terms entered by the user**.

front: Name the three stages by which a search engine works.
back: **Crawling**, **indexing** and **ranking**.

front: What happens during the crawling stage?
back: **Web crawlers scour the internet daily** to retrieve new websites.

front: What happens during the indexing stage?
back: Websites are **categorised** based on the **content of their web pages, keywords and metadata**.

front: What happens during the ranking stage?
back: Websites are **ranked and listed on search engine pages**, depending on many factors, so that the most relevant results are displayed.

front: How does filter software decide whether to allow a website?
back: It uses **two lists stored in a database**, and the URL entered by the user is **compared against both lists**.

front: URLs on the <u>**                **</u> are allowed and the website can be viewed, while URLs on the blacklist are blocked.
back: URLs on the **whitelist** are allowed and the website can be viewed, while URLs on the blacklist are blocked.

front:
**True or False?**

A URL that appears on neither the whitelist nor the blacklist is blocked.
back:
**False.**

URLs that cannot be found on **either list are allowed**.

front: Who uses filter software, and why?
back: Filter software is used by **schools and parents** to **protect children from accessing age inappropriate content**, and administrators can add and remove URLs from the lists.

front: Give four benefits of using a local area network.
back: Users can **share peripherals** such as printers, have **shared access to the internet**, **access their files from any computer** on the network, **communicate more easily**, **share files and folders**, use servers for **centralised backups, updates and security**, and use **media streaming**.

front: Why is sharing peripherals on a LAN a benefit?
back: Sharing peripherals **reduces the cost and time** needed to access a central one, rather than buying a device for every user.

front: Why is sharing data on a LAN a benefit?
back: Shared data allows **easier collaboration** between users.

front: What does flexible access on a LAN allow a user to do?
back: Flexible access allows **hot desking**, because users can access their files from **any computer on the network**.

front: Why is shared access to the internet a benefit of a LAN?
back: It **reduces the need for individual connectivity** for every device.

front: What three things can a server provide centrally on a LAN?
back: A server can provide centralised **backups**, **updates** and **security**.

front: Servers and switches can provide a central point of <u>**            **</u>, so users cannot complete tasks if one fails.
back: Servers and switches can provide a central point of **failure**, so users cannot complete tasks if one fails.

front: Give two security drawbacks of using a LAN.
back: There is an **increased security risk to data**, and **malicious software can infiltrate the network** and render it unusable.

front: What factors can affect the performance of a LAN?
back: Performance is affected by the **number of users** and the **amount of data on the network at one time**.

front:
**True or False?**

Connecting computers on a LAN removes the security risk to data.
back:
**False.**

A LAN brings an **increased security risk to data**, because malicious software can spread across the network.

front: Name two kinds of media a LAN can be used to stream.
back: A LAN can stream **movies**, **music** and **gaming** content.

front: Define **peer-to-peer network**.
back: A peer-to-peer network is a network with **no server providing services**, where every computer is **equal to all other computers**.

front: Name three things each peer on a peer-to-peer network is responsible for.
back: Each peer **provides access to its own files** and is responsible for its **own backups** and its **own security**, and often has its **own printer attached**.

front: Give three advantages of a peer-to-peer network.
back: It is **very easy to set up and maintain**, **very cheap** because there is no expensive hardware to purchase, and **no specialist knowledge or staff** are required to run it.

front: Give three disadvantages of a peer-to-peer network.
back: Users must **manage their own backups** and **their own software updates**, and the network **can be less secure**.

front: Why does a lack of centralised backup on a peer-to-peer network cost more?
back: **Each client has to be backed up separately**, so **individual backup devices** are needed on every device.

front: Why can users not hot-desk on a peer-to-peer network?
back: There are **no roaming profiles**, so a user's files and settings do not follow them to another machine.

front: Define **client-server network**.
back: A client-server network is a network that **uses a server**, with clients connecting to it via a **switch**.

front: Name four single purposes a server on a client-server network might have.
back: A server might **manage access to the internet**, **manage printing**, **provide email services**, **provide backups** or **control security**.

front: How does a server compare with the client machines on the network?
back: Servers are often **more powerful** than the client machines, are seen as **more significant**, and can require **specialist hardware and software**.

front: Give three advantages of a client-server network.
back: **Backups are easier** because they are done from one central point, **updating and installing software can be done centrally** rather than on each machine, and **security of files can be managed easily**.

front: A server can be a single point of <u>**            **</u>, meaning all users would lose access to the network if it fails.
back: A server can be a single point of **failure**, meaning all users would lose access to the network if it fails.

front: Give two cost-related disadvantages of a client-server network.
back: Servers can be **expensive to purchase, set up and maintain**, and a **specialist network manager** is required because servers need specialist IT knowledge.

front:
**True or False?**

Most schools and companies use a peer-to-peer network model.
back:
**False.**

Most companies, organisations and schools use a **client-server** model; it is most **homes** that use a peer-to-peer model.

front: What is the purpose of a password on a network?
back: A password acts as a **digital lock** to prevent unauthorised access to an account, and **authenticates a user** to the network.

front: Why are passwords stored in encrypted form in a database?
back: So that even with **unauthorised access to the database**, a hacker would **not be able to gain the individual passwords** of users.

front: Define **firewall**.
back: A firewall is a **barrier between a network and the internet** that prevents **unwanted traffic** from entering by **filtering requests** to ensure they are legitimate.

front: What is the difference between a hardware firewall and a software firewall?
back: A **hardware** firewall protects the **whole network**, while a **software** firewall protects the **individual devices**, monitoring the data going to and from each computer.

front: Define **encryption**.
back: Encryption is a method of **scrambling data** so that **unauthorised users cannot understand it**, using **keys** and complex mathematical algorithms.

front: How does symmetric encryption work?
back: The sender uses a key to **encrypt** the data before transmission, and the receiver uses the **same key** to **decrypt** it.

front: What is the main weakness of symmetric encryption?
back: The challenge of **securely sharing the key** — if an unauthorised user captures it, they can **decrypt all intercepted messages**.

front: How does public key encryption work?
back: The receiver **openly shares a public key** which the sender uses to **encrypt** the data, and only the receiver's **private key** can **decrypt** it.

front: Why is public key encryption used for passwords and bank details rather than large files?
back: It is **slower than symmetric encryption**, so it is used for **more secure and smaller data transactions**, while symmetric encryption is faster and suits large amounts of data.

front: What do WEP and WPA stand for?
back: WEP is **Wireless Encryption Protocol** and WPA is **Wi-Fi Protected Access**.

front: Why is WEP less secure than WPA?
back: With WEP **every device uses the same key**, so eavesdropping software can intercept data packets and **identify the key**, whereas WPA gives **each device a different key** and uses **new keys for every packet**.

front: Eavesdropping software known as packet <u>**            **</u> can intercept data packets and identify a WEP key.
back: Eavesdropping software known as packet **sniffers** can intercept data packets and identify a WEP key.

front: Define **virtual private network (VPN)**.
back: A VPN allows users to **remotely connect to private local area networks**, with **all data sent and received encrypted**.

front: Give three common uses of a VPN.
back: **Remotely accessing a company's network** when working from home, making **secure payments**, **hiding web activities**, and **bypassing geolocation rights management or online censorship**.

front: Name the four file access rights.
back: **Read** (view contents only), **write** (change contents or create new files), **delete** (remove files) and **execute** (run applications).

front: Define **transaction log**.
back: A transaction log is a **secure file on a network** that keeps a **record of every action performed by devices** on that network.

front:
**True or False?**

Transaction logs directly protect a network from attack.
back:
**False.**

Transaction logs **do not directly protect a network** — they help administrators **monitor and identify unusual activity**.

front: Name four things recorded in a transaction log.
back: **Device and data access**, **timestamps**, **user IDs**, and **successful and failed login attempts**.

front: Define **unauthorised access**.
back: Unauthorised access is when a user **gains access to a network without permission**.

front: What is the difference between direct and indirect entry?
back: **Direct entry** is a user trying to gain access themselves or with software that repeatedly tries username and password combinations, while **indirect entry** is **exploiting vulnerabilities** in software or users.

front: Software that repeatedly tries username and password combinations is carrying out a <u>**                    **</u> attack.
back: Software that repeatedly tries username and password combinations is carrying out a **brute force** attack.

front: Define **botnet**.
back: A botnet is a **group of computers used without their owners' knowledge** to carry out **harmful activities** or **spread malware**.

front: Give three ways accidental deletion of data can occur.
back: A user might **press the wrong key** on a keyboard, **format media on the wrong device**, or **lose power unexpectedly**.

front: Define **malware**.
back: Malware is any software created with **malicious intent to cause harm to a computer system**.

front: Give three issues caused by malware.
back: Files being **deleted, corrupted or encrypted**, the internet connection becoming **slow or unusable**, and the computer **crashing or shutting down**.

front: What is a virus?
back: A virus is a program which can **replicate itself** on a user's computer, containing code that causes **unwanted and unexpected events** such as corrupting files or deleting data.

front: What is the main difference between a worm and a virus?
back: A worm will **spread to other drives and computers on the network**, whereas a virus replicates on the computer it has infected.

front: What is a Trojan?
back: A Trojan **disguises itself as legitimate software** but contains **malicious code in the background**.

front: What can spyware do once it is on a device?
back: Spyware can **record the screen** and **log keystrokes** to gain access to **passwords**, allowing a person to spy on the user's activities.

front: What does ransomware do?
back: Ransomware **locks the computer and encrypts documents and other important files**, then makes a **demand for money** in return for the password to decrypt them.

front:
**True or False?**

Paying a ransomware demand guarantees the user will get their data back.
back:
**False.**

There is **no guarantee** that paying the ransom will result in the user getting their data back.

front: Define **phishing**.
back: Phishing is a form of **social engineering** that sends **fraudulent, legitimate-looking emails** to many addresses, claiming to be from a **reputable company**, to gain access to a user's details.

front: Why are phishing messages sent to many users at once?
back: It **increases the chances of a user responding**, because **not all users are vulnerable** and many people are aware of phishing.

front: Define **pharming**.
back: Pharming is when a user types a website address into a browser and is **redirected to a 'fake' website**, to trick them into typing in sensitive information such as passwords.

front: Give three ways pharming can be prevented.
back: **Keeping anti-malware software up to date**, **checking URLs regularly**, and **making sure the padlock icon is visible**.

front: Give four features of a strong password.
back: A strong password has **more than eight characters**, a **mixture of letters, numbers and symbols**, a **mixture of uppercase and lowercase letters**, and uses **uncommon words or phrases**.

front: Define **biometrics**.
back: Biometrics are a way of **authenticating a user by their unique human characteristics**, such as fingerprint scans, retina scans and facial recognition.

front: Give two advantages of biometrics over passwords.
back: Biometric data is **unique to the person and cannot be copied**, so it is always with them, and it **eliminates attacks such as shoulder surfing and key-logging**, whereas passwords can be copied, forgotten, guessed or cracked.

front: Give three disadvantages of biometrics.
back: They can be **intrusive**, **scans may not be recognised** (for example a fingerprint scan with dirty hands), they are **very expensive to install**, **low light affects facial recognition**, and people may be **uncomfortable having their characteristics stored in a database**.

front: What does a CAPTCHA test for?
back: A CAPTCHA tests whether a website request originates from a **human or a machine (bot)**.

front: Name the three types of CAPTCHA.
back: **Text**, where users decipher characters from a distorted text box, **image**, where users select all images containing a specific object, and **checkbox**, where a user confirms they are not a robot.

front: Name the three types of software combined in anti-malware.
back: **Anti-virus**, **anti-spam** and **anti-spyware**.

front: How does anti-malware software work?
back: It **scans email attachments, websites and downloaded files** for issues, blocks anything matching its list of known **malware signatures**, and **checks for updates** to keep its database current.

front: Name the three levels of access right a user can be given.
back: **Full access** to open, create, edit and delete files, **read-only access** to open files without editing or deleting, and **no access**, which hides the file from the user.

front: On what basis are access rights set?
back: Access rights are set based on a user's **role, responsibility or clearance level**.

front: How do access rights typically differ between staff and students on a school network?
back: Teaching staff are **partially restricted** and can access all student data but not other staff members' data, while students are **restricted** to their own data and files; administrators are **unrestricted**.

front: What does HTTP allow?
back: Hypertext Transfer Protocol allows communication between **clients and servers for website viewing**, letting clients **receive data** from the server and **send data** to it.

front: HTTPS works in the same way as HTTP, but all data sent and received is <u>**                    **</u>.
back: HTTPS works in the same way as HTTP, but all data sent and received is **encrypted**.

front: What is HTTPS used to protect?
back: HTTPS protects **sensitive information** such as **passwords, financial information and personal data**.

front: Give four warning signs that an email may be unsafe.
back: The email is from an **unknown sender**, the text is **general or impersonal**, it contains **spelling, punctuation or grammar mistakes**, attached files are **executable (.exe) files**, the tone is one of **urgency**, or the **URL is unrecognised**.

front: What is the difference between a full backup and an incremental backup?
back: A **full** backup copies **all files**, which is safest but slow, while an **incremental** backup copies **only files added or modified since the last backup**, which is faster but less secure.

front:
**True or False?**

Backups must always be run manually by the user.
back:
**False.**

Backups can be **automated and scheduled** to happen at less busy periods of the day, so they do not take up valuable system resources.

front: Where can backups be stored?
back: Backups can be stored **locally** on secondary storage or **remotely** in the cloud.

front: Define **online payment system**.
back: An online payment system **eliminates the need for physical cash** by facilitating the **payment for goods and services online**.

front: Name four benefits offered by online payment systems.
back: **Convenience**, since you can pay for anything, anytime, from anywhere; **security**, since encryption protects sensitive information; **increased reach** for international transactions; and **transparency**, since digital records are kept.

front: Why does transparency matter in an online payment system?
back: **Digital records are kept**, which makes it easy to **monitor payments and resolve disputes**.

front: Name the three most common types of online payment system.
back: **Third party payment processors**, **bank cards** and **contactless (NFC)** payments.

front: Third party payment processors facilitate online payments using an <u>**                    **</u> as identification.
back: Third party payment processors facilitate online payments using an **email address** as identification.

front: Why might a retailer link a third party payment processor to its online shop?
back: It makes the **purchasing process easier and faster** for the customer.

front: What three pieces of information from a bank card are required to make an online purchase?
back: The **16 digit card number**, the **expiry date** and the **security number (CVC)**.

front: What role do other financial institutions play when a bank card is used online?
back: They may be used to **authenticate the transaction**.

front: How does a contactless payment take place?
back: If a contactless card is in **close proximity of a reader** requesting a payment, the transaction can take place using **near field communication (NFC)**.

front: Why is there a limit on the amount of a contactless payment?
back: No extra authentication takes place, so the limit is there to **deter criminals**, because only **small amounts can be stolen**.

front: Why does NFC speed up the payment process?
back: Users can **scan or tap their card** rather than inserting it and **entering a PIN**, because NFC is a **contactless payment method**.

front: Name four ways online payments can be protected.
back: **Banks monitoring payments** and analysing spending patterns, **encryption**, **two factor authentication (2FA)**, and using **secure websites (HTTPS)**.

front:
**True or False?**

A contactless payment requires the user to enter a PIN for authentication.
back:
**False.**

**No extra authentication** takes place on a contactless payment, which is why the **amount is limited**.

front: Name the three biggest impacts of the internet on employment.
back: A **change in skills requirements**, **new job opportunities** and **job losses**.

front: How has automation changed the skills employers look for?
back: There is a **shift in the need for particular skill sets**, so employees must be **adaptable**, with a focus on **problem solving and critical thinking** rather than tasks that can now be automated.

front: Name three soft skills that have grown in importance.
back: **Effective communication**, **collaboration** and **lifelong learning**.

front: Name four new job areas created by the internet.
back: **Cyber security**, **data science**, **artificial intelligence and machine learning**, **digital marketing** and **cloud computing**.

front: What does someone working in data science do?
back: They **analyse data and extract insights**, which requires **programming knowledge**.

front: Name three areas of work within digital marketing.
back: **Content creation**, **search engine optimisation (SEO)** and **social media marketing**.

front: Why might the internet lead to job losses?
back: Employees who **do not improve their skills** may **not have the skills required** for new work, and if they are **unwilling to retrain** this may lead to job losses.

front: Define **working practices**.
back: Working practices are the **ways in which a person goes about completing a task** as part of their job.

front: What does collaborative working mean?
back: Employees can **work on the same project or task at the same time, in real time**, working together remotely.

front: Remote collaboration allows employers to choose employees from a much wider <u>**            **</u> pool.
back: Remote collaboration allows employers to choose employees from a much wider **talent** pool.

front: Give three advantages of collaborative working.
back: **Efficiency**, since tasks are completed more quickly; **knowledge**, from shared skills and experience; **creativity**, from other perspectives and team problem solving; and **morale**, from building team spirit.

front: Give three disadvantages of collaborative working.
back: **Co-ordination** is hard, since organising meetings and keeping people aligned is difficult; **personality clashes** can hinder progress; and **contribution** may be unequal between members.

front: What does flexible working mean?
back: Employees can **work when it suits them**, deciding **the hours they work** or **working from home**, and the internet also makes **working on the move** an option.

front: Give three advantages of flexible working.
back: A better **work life balance**, since work can be scheduled around personal commitments; higher **productivity**, since people work when they feel most productive; and **fewer sick days**.

front:
**True or False?**

Flexible working makes supervising and monitoring employees easier.
back:
**False.**

**Management** is one of its disadvantages — supervising and monitoring employees can be **more difficult**, alongside weaker **communication** and **isolation** from the social side of an office.

front: What kind of information can individuals keep up to date with online, and when?
back: Individuals can keep up to date with **news, sport and weather** information **24 hours a day**.

front: How does the availability of internet content compare with television and radio?
back: Television and radio are **broadcast at set times**, while the internet offers **24/7 availability**.

front: How does the choice of content on the internet compare with television and radio?
back: Television and radio have a **limited number of channels**, while the internet offers **millions of channels**.

front: Who decides what content appears on television and radio, compared with the internet?
back: On television and radio **editors decide on content** and it is **held to a standard**, while internet content is **not always edited** and **not always held to any standards**.

front: How does the reach of television and radio compare with the internet?
