back: Television and radio are **only available within range of a transmitter**, while the internet can be **accessed from anywhere with a connection**.

front: Some internet content is not openly available everywhere because it is <u>**                    **</u>.
back: Some internet content is not openly available everywhere because it is **geo-restricted**.

front: Name four new ways of learning the internet has made possible.
back: **Virtual learning environments (VLEs)**, **social learning**, **gamification** and **virtual reality (VR)**.

front: What does a virtual learning environment provide?
back: A VLE provides **online support from teachers and students**.

front: What does gamification do for learning?
back: Gamification makes learning **engaging and interactive**, promoting **knowledge retention**.

front: What does virtual reality offer a learner?
back: VR gives **immersive experiences**, **bringing abstract concepts to life**.

front: Name three types of on-demand content the internet gives access to.
back: Streaming of **movies**, **television** and **music**.

front:
**True or False?**

Information published on the internet is always edited and held to a standard.
back:
**False.**

Internet content is **not always edited** and **not always held to any standards**, unlike television and radio where editors decide on content.

front: Define **social interaction**.
back: Social interaction is **communication with and reaction to others**, and the internet has given users **different ways to participate socially**.

front: Name four ways the internet allows people to interact socially.
back: **Online gaming**, **video**, **instant messaging**, **social networking**, and **online spaces for work and learning**.

front: How does online interaction help people who feel isolated?
back: It provides **social support** and a **sense of belonging**, which is important for people who feel isolated or struggle with mental health.

front: Give two further arguments in favour of online social interaction.
back: **Connection and community**, since users connect with people who share their interests regardless of location; **expression**, since platforms give space to explore yourself freely; **convenience**, since it needs no travel and works 24/7; and **social change**, since it is a powerful tool for activism and raising awareness.

front: How can algorithms make online interaction harmful?
back: Algorithms can **limit exposure to diverse perspectives** and help **spread misinformation**.

front: Why can social comparison online damage mental health?
back: Users are **constantly comparing themselves to others**, which can lead to **low self esteem and poor mental health**.

front: Give two further arguments against online social interaction.
back: **Privacy** concerns over where shared data is kept and who has access; **distraction**, since notifications hinder productivity; and **addiction**, since too much interaction can be addictive.

front: Define **cyberbullying**.
back: Cyberbullying is **using the internet to send text, images or multimedia in order to upset or embarrass someone**.

front: Give three forms cyberbullying can take.
back: **Hurtful messages**, **distributing upsetting images**, and **preventing participation in online events or discussions**, which isolates the victim.

front:
**True or False?**

The anonymity of the internet means cyberbullies cannot be traced.
back:
**False.**

Cyberbullies **can feel protected** by the apparent anonymity of the internet, but most online communication is **easily monitored**.

front: Why is cyberbullying more damaging than bullying that happens offline?
back: It can **spread very quickly** and **to more people**.

front: Why has access to online goods and services reduced physical activity?
back: People **do not need to leave the comfort of their houses**, which has negative effects on their **health** and **wellbeing**.

front: Name three health effects of reduced physical activity.
back: An **increased risk of chronic diseases**, **musculoskeletal problems**, a **weakened immune system**, **metabolic issues** and **increased blood pressure**.

front: Reduced physical activity harms wellbeing through increased anxiety and depression, lower energy levels and poor <u>**            **</u> quality.
back: Reduced physical activity harms wellbeing through increased anxiety and depression, lower energy levels and poor **sleep** quality.

front: Where did workers traditionally have to go to access computer systems?
back: Workers traditionally accessed computer systems from an **office environment**, which is a **centralised** approach.

front: Why did common office hours such as 09:00 to 17:00 develop?
back: They developed to **facilitate access** to the centralised computer systems that workers needed.

front: What change in digital devices made working from home possible?
back: Digital devices became **cheaper and more powerful**, so they were increasingly **used at home**.

front: Working from home is a <u>**                    **</u> approach, rather than the traditional centralised one.
back: Working from home is a **decentralised** approach, rather than the traditional centralised one.

front: Name three things a digital device at home lets a worker do.
back: **Run a range of software**, **access the internet**, and **access online systems and applications**.

front: Give three benefits to an organisation of employees working from home.
back: It can **attract a talented, motivated workforce**, **employ from a wider location** including internationally, remove the need to **buy or rent office space**, remove **commuting and lateness**, and workers **may work more effectively**.

front: Give three drawbacks to an organisation of employees working from home.
back: **Concerns about data security**, it is **more difficult to manage and support employees**, **employees might not work as hard**, and there are **complications with payroll** for workers in different countries.

front: Give three benefits to an employee of working from home.
back: **No travel to work**, which means less stress and saves money; **more time working or resting**; the ability to **work at a time to suit them**; **fewer distractions**; a **comfortable environment**; the chance to **organise work around social or family commitments**; and **no uniform or business clothes** to buy.

front: Give three drawbacks to an employee of working from home.
back: **Distractions at home** from family and leisure activities, a **lack of social interaction**, and feeling **disconnected from the company**.

front: Why does the internet always being available benefit a home worker?
back: Because it is always available, they can **work at times suitable to them**.

front: How does collaborating online positively affect a home worker?
back: It lets them **share expertise**, **reduce the time to complete a task** and **share the workload**.

front: Why does access to a wider range of sources help a home worker?
back: It allows them to **make better decisions**.

front:
**True or False?**

Working from home is a benefit to employees only, not to the organisation.
back:
**False.**

It benefits **both** — organisations save on office space and can recruit internationally, while employees save travel time and gain flexibility.

front: Name the four positive impacts of the internet on organisations.
back: **Improved communication**, **access to global markets**, **access to a global workforce**, and changes in **how information is managed and used**.

front: Name four ways an organisation can communicate with its customers online.
back: Through **websites**, **email**, **instant messaging** and **social media**, easily and in **real time**.

front: Name three costs an organisation can reduce by selling products online.
back: **Overheads** such as rent, utilities and staff, **packaging**, and **postal charges**.

front: How does the internet widen an organisation's access to a workforce?
back: Organisations can **find and hire the best talent regardless of location**, be **more selective** rather than limited to travelling distance, select employees from **different time zones**, and possibly **reduce costs** where wages are lower.

front: Where does the big data organisations analyse come from?
back: From **smartphones**, **online applications**, **social media** and **payment systems**.

front: Organisations analyse big data to find <u>**                    **</u> of behaviour.
back: Organisations analyse big data to find **patterns** of behaviour.

front: What two things does analysing big data allow an organisation to improve?
back: It allows them to **improve the customer experience** and **improve process efficiency**.

front: Name the two negative impacts of the internet on organisations.
back: **Security issues** and **greater competition**.

front: How was organisational data traditionally kept secure?
back: It was kept in a **secure central location** using physical safety measures such as **walls**, **locks**, **alarms** and **security guards**.

front: Name the three ways employees typically access secure organisational data remotely.
back: Through a **VPN** to remotely access data on servers, by **transferring a copy** of the data home via external storage or email, or by storing the data on **someone else's server** in the cloud.

front: What prevents unauthorised users intercepting data being transferred on the internet?
back: **Encryption**.

front: How does an organisation guard against employees revealing login details?
back: By having **policies** that ensure employees are **accountable for their actions**.

front: Why does the internet drive down prices for consumers?
back: Consumers can **buy from organisations globally** rather than only local ones, and this **extra competition** drives down prices.

front: Name three industries put at risk by the internet, and what threatened each.
back: **Music and film rental** by online downloads and streaming, **record labels** because independent artists can release their own music online, **estate agents** by online advertising and virtual viewings, **newspaper publishers** by online news services, and **postal services** because messages and digital media can be sent instantly.

front:
**True or False?**

Before the internet, organisations competed globally for customers.
back:
**False.**

Traditionally organisations were only in competition with others in their **local area or country**; the internet opened competition up globally.

front: Name three forms of mass communication affected by less-restricted networks.
back: **Broadcasting**, **publishing** and **the internet**.

front: How did an individual get a message to the masses before the internet?
back: They would need to **persuade a media outlet to broadcast their message**, which made it **difficult to reach the masses**.

front: How have social media and video streaming changed who can broadcast a message?
back: They have given society a **platform to share their own messages to a global audience**.

front: Who or what controls what online content a user sees?
back: **Moderators** and **service owners** control what can be published, and **algorithms** determine what watchers see based on their **browsing history and online activity**.

front: Why does paid promotion reach more people?
back: **Paid promotion will be seen by more users** than content from individuals who do not pay.

front: What has been lost from user-generated reference sites?
back: They have **removed the element of fact checking by experts or editors**, so users can contribute content that **may or may not be true**.

front: Give one negative impact of less-restricted networks on law enforcement.
back: Social media and video messaging services can be used to **organise illegal activities while avoiding police**.

front: Give three positive impacts of less-restricted networks on law enforcement.
back: A network of **CCTV cameras** records illegal actions, **footage captured on social media** helps identify suspects, and social media is used to **organise events to support victims**.

front: Define **the information gap**.
back: The information gap is the **divide created between people who have access to online information and those who do not**.

front: What does being information rich give a person?
back: **Good access to information**, which **improves their education** and helps **enable them to make decisions**.

front: Being information poor means reduced access to information, which decreases education and reduces the ability to make <u>**                    **</u>.
back: Being information poor means reduced access to information, which decreases education and reduces the ability to make **decisions**.

front:
**True or False?**

The information gap was created by the internet.
back:
**False.**

The gap has existed **since television and radio were introduced**; the internet has **further widened** it.

front: Define **the digital divide**.
back: The digital divide is the **gap between people who have access to digital devices and the internet and people who do not**.

front: Name four factors that affect a person's access to digital technology.
back: **Economy and infrastructure**, **location**, **politics**, **religion**, **disability** and **social** factors.

front: How does a country's economy affect access to the internet?
back: Countries with a **strong economy can invest in infrastructure** that provides access, while countries with **emerging and developing economies may prioritise other needs** such as food and healthcare.

front: How does location affect access to digital technology?
back: People who live in **remote locations** may be somewhere **wireless signals or cabling cannot reach**.

front: Give two ways politics can restrict access to information.
back: **Government control** can mean **not allowing access to certain websites or content from other countries**, and **blocking access to satellites** to stop television and radio broadcasts because of cultural influences.

front: Why can disability contribute to the digital divide?
back: Some digital devices are **not inclusive**.

front: Social factors affecting access include age, gender, education and <u>**                    **</u>.
back: Social factors affecting access include age, gender, education and **income**.

front: How have traditional ways of socialising changed?
back: Meeting in person and talking have been **replaced with an increased use of digital devices**.

front: Give one benefit of the way the internet has changed socialising.
back: The internet allows people to **connect with other people around the world**.

front: Give two negative effects of using digital devices to socialise.
back: It can lead to **isolation** and **anxiety around meeting people in real life**.

front:
**True or False?**

The digital divide is caused only by whether a person can afford a device.
back:
**False.**

Income is one **social** factor, but access is also affected by **economy and infrastructure**, **location**, **politics**, **religion** and **disability**.

front: Define **online community**.
back: An online community is a **group of people with a shared common interest who communicate online**.

front: What two things does every online community have?
back: A **function**, which is what it does for the people who use it, and **features**, which are what enable it to function.

front: What is the function of a social networking community?
back: To **allow users to connect through shared interests or relationships**.

front: How were social networking communities traditionally separated?
back: Into **personal** and **professional** communities.

front: What appears on a user's stream, wall or timeline?
back: **Messages from friends and groups**, usually the **first thing a user sees when logged in**, ordered **chronologically**.

front: What happens to the content of a user's status updates?
back: It is **stored by social network providers** and can be used for **targeted advertising**.

front: What can happen when users share other people's posts?
back: Sharing opens a post or comment to a **wider audience**, which can lead to it **going viral**.

front: What do tags allow a social networking user to do?
back: Tags allow content to be **categorised**, and users can **search for tags to find content**.

front: How does a platform decide which users to suggest you connect with?
back: Users with **similar interests or shared personal or professional experiences** are suggested.

front: What is the function of online gaming?
back: To **allow users to play multiplayer games together** over the internet or a computer network.

front: What are experience points and trophies for in online gaming?
back: They are **rewards for in-game achievements** that **motivate users to continue to play**.

front: Name three other features of an online gaming community.
back: **Links to social media**, **user profiles** that showcase achievements, **how-to guides and in-game tutorials**, **discussion boards or forums**, and **notifications**.

front: What is the function of an online work space?
back: To give users a platform to **collaborate together for the purposes of work**, bringing remote teams and projects together.

front: Name four features of an online work space.
back: **Cloud storage**, **commenting** directly in documents and tasks, a **messaging system**, **shared calendars**, a **contacts list**, **chat rooms**, and **virtual meeting spaces**.

front: A VLE is an online platform for <u>**                    **</u> and training.
back: A VLE is an online platform for **education** and training.

front: What is the function of a virtual learning environment?
back: To give **teachers and students a shared platform** to use **learning and assessment features**.

front:
**True or False?**

Quizzes in a virtual learning environment must be marked by the teacher.
back:
**False.**

Quizzes and multiple choice tests in a VLE are **self marking** and are **graded automatically**.

front: Define **user-generated reference site**.
back: A user-generated reference site is an **information website created and maintained by communities of users**, such as wikis and forums.

front: What is the function of a wiki?
back: To allow users to **contribute to a community website or database**, **collaborating** to build and edit web pages.

front: Name three features of a wiki.
back: **User accounts**, which track edits and who made them; an **editor** for making changes and adding content; and **search tools** for finding content quickly.

front: What is the function of a forum?
back: To provide users with an **online space for structured discussions**.

front: What is the difference between a moderator and an administrator on a forum?
back: **Moderators** manage discussions and **enforce rules to keep order**, while **administrators** are **in control of the entire forum**, managing users and introducing new features.

front: What is the difference between a post and a thread?
back: A **post** is a user's message that contributes to a thread, while a **thread** is a **collection of posts about a specific topic**.

front: <u>**                    **</u> automatically removes forum content that violates the rules or is inappropriate.
back: **Censoring** automatically removes forum content that violates the rules or is inappropriate.

front: What do reports and flags allow forum users to do?
back: They allow users to **notify moderators about problematic content**.

front: Define **user-generated content**.
back: User-generated content is content **made by users of sites and services** and **available online**, such as video and photo sharing sites, blogs and vlogs.

front: What is the function of video and photo sharing sites?
back: To allow users to **access and share content created by each other**, creating a **sense of community**.

front: What does a content management system provide on a sharing site?
back: It provides tools for **uploading, organising, editing and sharing content**.

front: What do tags do on a video or photo sharing site?
back: Tags allow users to **add keywords** that help **categorise and discover content**.

front: What is the function of a social bookmarking site?
back: To give users a platform to **categorise and share web documents and URLs**.

front:
**True or False?**

Third party integration on a sharing or bookmarking site keeps content within that one platform.
back:
**False.**

Third party integration **connects with other social media platforms for wider sharing**.

front: What does data protection legislation do?
back: It **protects personal data from being misused**.

front: Give four examples of personal data.
back: **Name**, **address**, **date of birth**, **race** and **religion**.

front: Under the data protection principles, what must personal data be collected for?
back: **Specified and lawful purposes** — an organisation **cannot use personal data for any purpose other than the one it originally stated**, and cannot pass it on without permission.

front: Why can a bank not ask a new customer about their previous trips?
back: Personal data must be **adequate, relevant and not excessive**, so an organisation **cannot request personal data it does not need right away**.

front: What right does a person have if an organisation holds data about them that is wrong or out of date?
back: Personal data must be **kept accurate and up to date**, so they have a **right to have it corrected or deleted**.

front: Personal data will not be kept for longer than is <u>**                    **</u>, so an organisation must delete it once it no longer has a need for it.
back: Personal data will not be kept for longer than is **necessary**, so an organisation must delete it once it no longer has a need for it.

front: What must an organisation do if a person requests the personal data held on them?
back: Personal data must be **processed in line with people's rights**, so the organisation must **provide them with all the personal data it holds** on them.

front: Name three common exemptions from data protection rules.
back: **Domestic purposes**, such as writing to friends and family or taking pictures for your own enjoyment; **law enforcement**, such as police investigating a crime; and **intelligence services processing**.

front: What does copyright legislation protect?
back: It protects the **intellectual property of an individual or a company**, making it **illegal to copy, modify or distribute** software or other intellectual property **without the relevant permission**.

front: When is copyright applied to an original work, and how long does it last?
back: Copyright is **automatically applied** to original work and does not expire until **25 to 70 years from the death of the creator**, depending on the type of work.

front: Whose responsibility is it to act when a work has been copied?
back: It is the **creator's own responsibility** to take action.

front: Name three primary breaches of copyright.
back: **Copying an original work**, **issuing a copy to the public**, **renting or lending a copy to the public**, **performing, showing or playing the work in public**, and **making an adaptation** of it.

front: Define **software piracy**.
back: Software piracy is the **illegal copying and distribution of software**.

front: Name three methods companies use to prevent software piracy.
back: A **product key or licence** to activate the software, an **agreement of terms and conditions** the user must accept before installing, and **holograms** on packaging that are too difficult and costly for pirates to copy.

front: Give three examples of a copyright exemption.
back: Uses **for the benefit of people with a disability**, **non-commercial research or private study**, **recordings of broadcasts for archiving**, **copies made by a library, educational establishment, museum or archive**, and use in a **parody**.

front: Name four ways an individual can be monitored using digital technology.
back: **CCTV**, **automatic number plate recognition (ANPR)**, **physical forms of identification**, **network activity** such as IP and MAC addresses, **GPS data shared by apps**, and **GPS trackers**.

front:
**True or False?**

Monitoring individuals with digital technology brings benefits but no drawbacks.
back:
**False.**

It **compromises people's privacy**, is **expensive to set up, monitor and maintain**, **consumes energy**, and can **make the public feel they are not trusted**.

front: Name four health issues caused by prolonged use of IT.
back: **Repetitive strain injury (RSI)**, **back and neck problems**, **eye strain** and **headaches**.

front: What causes repetitive strain injury?
back: Damage to the **fingers, wrists and joints**, traditionally caused by **prolonged use of a keyboard and mouse**.

front: Give three ways to prevent repetitive strain injury.
back: Have the **correct posture**, **use a wrist support** if necessary, **take regular breaks**, and make use of **ergonomic keyboards**.

front: Give three ways to prevent back and neck problems.
back: Use **adjustable chairs**, **take regular breaks** and use a **foot rest**.

front: What causes eye strain?
back: **Staring at a computer screen for prolonged periods** or **incorrect lighting causing reflections**.

front: Give three ways to prevent eye strain.
back: **Take regular breaks**, use an **anti-glare screen filter**, and **change from a CRT to an LCD monitor**.

front: Name four factors that combine to cause headaches when using IT.
back: **Poor lighting**, **flickering screens**, **reflections** and **fatigue**.

front: Define **physical safety**.
back: Physical safety is **creating a safe environment when using technology**, considering dangers that could lead to **serious injury or loss of life** and identifying strategies to mitigate them.

front: Name four physical safety risks of using ICT.
back: **Electrocution** from spilling drinks near electrical equipment, **fire hazard** from overloading plug sockets, **equipment overheating**, **trailing cables** as a trip hazard, and **heavy equipment falling**.

front: Give three ways to reduce the risk of electrocution.
back: **Keep liquids away** from electrical equipment, ensure cables are **properly insulated and protected**, **turn off and unplug equipment before cleaning or maintenance**, and use **circuit breakers or fuses** to prevent electrical overload.

front: Give three ways to reduce the risk of fire from overloaded sockets.
back: Use **surge protectors**, ensure there are **enough plug sockets** in the room, **do not plug too many devices into the same socket**, and **do not leave devices plugged in and unattended**.

front: Give three ways to stop equipment overheating.
back: Ensure equipment is **properly ventilated and not obstructed**, keep **flammable materials away from heat sources**, **do not cover air vents**, and **regularly check equipment** for signs of wear or damage.

front: Cables that are not properly secured or organised create a <u>**            **</u> hazard.
back: Cables that are not properly secured or organised create a **trip** hazard.

front: Give three ways to reduce trip hazards from cables.
back: Use **cable ties or clips**, **keep cables away from walkways**, **secure cables under desks**, use **cable covers**, and where possible **use wireless devices** to reduce cables.

front:
**True or False?**

Taking regular breaks helps with only one of the four common health issues.
back:
**False.**

Taking regular breaks is a prevention for **RSI**, **back and neck problems**, **eye strain** and **headaches** — all four.

front: Define **online safety**.
back: Online safety is **knowing about and using the internet safely and responsibly**, and knowing how to **protect yourself from potential dangers and threats**.

front: Name four activities online safety applies to.
back: Using the **internet**, **email**, **social media** and **online gaming**.

front: Why does online safety matter for a person's digital reputation?
back: Being **mindful of online behaviour and interactions** protects a digital reputation, which can have **long-term consequences in personal and professional lives**.

front: How does online safety support overall wellbeing?
back: It helps maintain a **healthy balance between online and offline lives**, reducing the risk of **addiction, mental health issues, or negative impacts on relationships and self-esteem**.

front: Give three ways to stay safe when using the internet.
back: Use **trusted websites** recommended by teachers or reputable sources, use **search engines that allow only age-appropriate websites** along with **filters**, and **never reveal personal information**.

front: What are the dangers of opening or replying to emails from unknown people?
back: The email or its **attachments** may carry **phishing** attempts or **spam**.

front: What should a user check before sending personal data or images by email?
back: They should **know who the email is for**, send only to **people they know**, and avoid **identifiable content** such as school photos.

front: Give three ways to stay safe when using social media.
back: Know how to **block and report** people sending unwanted content, know where the **privacy settings** are, **only accept friend requests from people you know**, and **do not post images or details that can be used to locate you**.

front: What advice applies to meeting an online contact face to face?
back: **Do not meet anyone you do not know**; if you do, **take an adult** and **meet publicly**.

front: Give three ways to stay safe when playing games online.
back: **Do not use real names as usernames**, **never share personal or financial details** with other players, and know how to **block and report players** for inappropriate messages or comments.

front: What do privacy settings on a social media platform let a user control?
back: They **limit who can access or view personal information and posts**, reducing the number of people who can see posts or images.

front:
**True or False?**

It is safe to share a friend's personal data online as long as you trust the people who will see it.
back:
**False.**

Users must **respect the confidentiality of personal data belonging to other people**.

front: Define **acceptable behaviour policy**.
back: An acceptable behaviour policy is a **set of rules** that outlines **how people are expected to conduct themselves online**.

front: An acceptable behaviour policy typically covers desired behaviours, unacceptable behaviours, reporting procedures and <u>**                    **</u>.
back: An acceptable behaviour policy typically covers desired behaviours, unacceptable behaviours, reporting procedures and **consequences**.

front: Where are acceptable behaviour policies used?
back: They are used in **all forms of online community**.

front: Name the four key areas of environmental impact of digital technology.
back: **Carbon footprint**, **e-waste**, **resource consumption** and **energy use**.

front: Which three stages of a device's life add to greenhouse gas emissions?
back: The **production**, the **use** and the **disposal** of digital technology.

front: Where does e-waste often end up, and why is that a problem?
back: It often ends up in **landfills in less developed countries**, leading to **health and pollution hazards**.

front: A throw-away society generates a growing amount of <u>**            **</u>.
back: A throw-away society generates a growing amount of **e-waste**.

front: What does resource consumption refer to in digital technology?
back: **Rare materials and resources being consumed** during the **manufacturing of digital devices**.

front: What is putting extra strain on power grids?
back: The **increased use of data centres** and the **growing number of digital devices in the home**.

front: Give two ways of reducing the environmental impact of devices at home and in the office.
back: **Using renewable energies** and **using more energy efficient devices**.

front: Why are data centres an environmental problem?
back: They require **extensive cooling**, which is generated using **non-renewable energies**.

front: Give two ways of reducing the environmental impact of a data centre.
back: **Geolocating data centres in colder climates**, and siting them **near rivers to make use of natural hydro-electric power**.

front: Give three ways of mitigating the poisonous substances used in digital devices.
back: **Recycling**, **education**, **laws** and finding **harmless alternatives**.

front: Give one environmental benefit of buying a previously-owned device.
back: It is **more sustainable** because **fewer precious metals are mined**, it **reduces waste materials leaking into the ground, water supply and food chain**, and it means **non-renewable resources such as oil are not depleted** because less plastic is used.

front:
**True or False?**

A device only affects the environment while it is being used.
back:
**False.**

The **production**, **use** and **disposal** of a device all contribute to its carbon footprint, and disposal also creates **e-waste**.

front: Define **primary source**.
back: A primary source is a source that **you have created yourself**.

front: Define **secondary source**.
back: A secondary source is a source that has been **created by someone else**.

front: Give three examples of a primary source.
back: **Sound recordings**, **photographs**, **interviews or questionnaires**, **social media posts** and **emails** that you have created yourself.

front: Give three examples of a secondary source.
back: **Newspapers**, **books**, **television and radio broadcasts**, **websites**, and **CDs, DVDs or Blu-rays**.

front: What two things must you consider when selecting the most appropriate source of information?
back: Its **fitness for purpose** and its **fitness for the intended audience**.

front: Name five features that help you use a search engine effectively.
back: **Keywords**, **search types**, **search tools**, **suggested sites and autofill**, and **search syntax**.

front: What are search types used for?
back: They **refine your search**, for example searching specifically for **images**, **news** or **location**.

front: What do search tools do?
back: They provide **filters and sorting options** to **narrow down searches**.

front: What does the AND (+) operator do in a search?
back: It returns **only results that match both words**.

front: Putting a minus sign before a word tells a search engine to return results that do <u>**            **</u> include that word.
back: Putting a minus sign before a word tells a search engine to return results that do **not** include that word.

front: What do quotation marks do in a search?
back: Matching with quotation marks **only displays results that include the whole phrase**.

front: Why might a user filter search results by usage rights?
back: To **comply with copyright**.

front:
**True or False?**

All search engines return the same results for the same search terms.
back:
**False.**

Different search engines **use different processes and algorithms**, which is why using more than one can be an effective strategy.

front: What does it mean to evaluate information?
back: To evaluate information you **check it is fit for purpose**.

front: Name the five things you check when evaluating a source.
back: Its **accuracy**, **age**, **relevance**, **reliability** and **bias**.

front: How do you check the accuracy of a source?
back: Check that it is from a **reputable source**, that the information **matches other reputable sources**, and that the source **provides evidence**.

front: Why does the age of a source matter?
back: Checking the **publication date** shows whether information is **old or now false**, or **too recent**.

front: How do you check the reliability of a source?
back: **Compare the information against other sources** of the same information — if it **does not match** it could be **false or inaccurate**.

front: Give three questions to ask when checking a source for bias.
back: Does the source **consider different viewpoints**? Is it **just facts or does it give extra context**? If it contains **data or statistics, where did they come from**?

front: What is the risk of using a biased source?
back: The information could be **prejudiced**, or **only look at one side of an argument or viewpoint**.

front: What does copyright legislation make illegal?
back: It makes it illegal to **copy, modify or distribute software or other intellectual property without the relevant permission**.

front: Why do free downloads of copyrighted material harm the creator?
back: They **prevent the intellectual copyright holder from earning their income** on the work they have created.

front: Define **plagiarism**.
back: Plagiarism is **presenting information or ideas from another source as your own**, without **giving credit to the original author**.

front: Give a common example of digital plagiarism.
back: **Copying and pasting from the internet** without stating where the information came from.

front: To avoid plagiarism a user should <u>**                    **</u> or rephrase information in their own words.
back: To avoid plagiarism a user should **rewrite** or rephrase information in their own words.

front: What must you always state to avoid plagiarism?
back: Always state **where the information came from**, which can be the **author's name** or the **URL** it was found on.

front:
**True or False?**

Plagiarism only counts if the person meant to pass the work off as their own.
back:
**False.**

Plagiarism can be done **intentionally and unintentionally** — failing to state who information belongs to is plagiarism either way.

front: Name the four characteristics of a shopping website.
back: A **product catalogue**, a **basket**, a **checkout** and **secure payments**.

front: Why are product catalogues grouped into categories?
back: Grouping into categories **makes browsing easier** for the customer.

front: What is the purpose of a basket on a shopping site?
back: It allows a user to **add multiple items** and keep them **in one place** until they are ready to **pay in full in one transaction**.

front: Name two things a user can do at checkout besides paying.
back: **Edit delivery details** and **use voucher codes**.

front: What two options does a checkout usually give a user before completing a purchase?
back: To **sign in** or to **proceed as a guest** on the site.

front: Secure payment on a shopping site is often handled by a <u>**                    **</u> payment processor.
back: Secure payment on a shopping site is often handled by a **third-party** payment processor.

front: Why are catalogues linked to one another on a shopping site?
back: So that **similar recommendations** can be made for the user during their shopping experience.

front: Give four advantages of online shopping to the customer.
back: A **wider choice of sellers** and **of products**, **no need to travel**, the ability to **build a profile** and **check availability**, **24/7 shopping**, **targeted marketing** giving relevant recommendations, **no queuing**, and **easier price comparison**.

front: Give four disadvantages of online shopping to the customer.
back: **Security concerns**, **limited physical interaction** with products, **delivery delays and fees**, and **impersonal customer service**.

front: Why can a customer compare prices more easily online than in shops?
back: There is a **wider choice of sellers**, and the customer **does not have to travel** between them.

front:
**True or False?**

A shopping site basket requires the user to pay for each item as a separate transaction.
back:
**False.**

A basket keeps everything **in one place** so the user can **pay in full for their entire purchase in one transaction**.

front: What can a customer do once they select an item from the product catalogue?
back: They can **add it to their basket**.

front: Define **online booking system**.
back: An online booking system is a computer system that **allows customers to purchase tickets for events online**.

front: Name the two main industries that use online booking systems.
back: **Travel**, for booking flights, hotels and package holidays, and **entertainment**, covering music, film and leisure or sport.

front: Give four advantages of an online booking system to the customer.
back: **Convenience and 24/7 booking**, **instant confirmation and ticketing**, the ability to **compare prices and options**, **promotions and personalised offers**, it is **faster to change or cancel**, **automated reminders** by email or text, and **repeated bookings** are easy to make.

front: Give four disadvantages of an online booking system.
back: **Technical issues and downtime**, **security and privacy concerns**, **transaction and booking fees**, **impersonal customer service**, the need for an **internet connected device**, and **staff may lose their jobs**.

front: Give one benefit of an online booking system to the business rather than the customer.
back: **Staff are freed up to do other things**.

front: What happens after a customer chooses a film and a date on a cinema booking site?
back: The **database is searched** and the **times and availability are displayed** on the screen.

front: What is displayed once a customer chooses a suitable time?
back: The **screen seating chart**, showing which seats are **available and which are taken**.

front: Once a customer selects a seat, it is <u>**                    **</u> made unavailable for booking by any other user.
back: Once a customer selects a seat, it is **temporarily** made unavailable for booking by any other user.

front: What is output to the customer once payment is taken?
back: A **confirmation message is displayed**, and a **payment receipt and QR code e-ticket are emailed**.

front: What is the final step in the cinema booking process?
back: The **database is updated** to make the seats **unavailable**.

front: When a flight booking is made, what is the booking database searched for?
back: The **customer reference number**, then **matching departure airports** and **matching destination airports**, and finally whether **seats or tickets are available**.

front: What happens to the seat count when a flight booking is confirmed?
back: The seat is **flagged as booked** and the **number of seats available is reduced** by the number booked.

front: What is output if no seats are available on a requested flight?
back: An **error message** is output.

front:
**True or False?**

Online booking systems benefit customers only, and bring no risks to a business.
back:
**False.**

Businesses face **technical issues and downtime**, **security and privacy concerns**, and the customer service they give becomes **impersonal and less tailored**.

front: Define **internet banking**.
back: Internet banking is a **secure online platform for accessing and controlling a person's bank account**.

front: Give two ways a customer can access internet banking.
back: Through a **secure website** on the internet, or by using the **bank's official app** on a smartphone.

front: Name four things a customer can do with internet banking.
back: **Transfers**, **bill payments**, **account management**, checking a **balance**, ordering **cards or chequebooks**, reporting cards **lost or stolen**, setting up a **new account** and making **loan applications**.

front: Name four features of an online banking service.
back: **Increased access** to chat, support or service at any time; **encryption** giving secure payments and data transfer; **anti-fraud measures** such as matching the name of a payee; **instant mobile notifications**; and the ability to carry out **multiple transactions simultaneously with no queuing**.

front: Give four advantages of internet banking.
back: **Convenience and 24/7 access**, **easy account management**, a **reduced need for branch visits** saving time and money, potentially **better interest rates**, **secure transactions using encryption**, and it is **easier to shop around** for the best account.

front: Give four disadvantages of internet banking.
back: It **requires a reliable internet connection**, there is **more risk of fraud**, it is **easier to make errors** by typing in the wrong information, and **physical cash cannot be deposited or withdrawn**.

front: Internet banking secures transactions and payments using <u>**                    **</u>.
back: Internet banking secures transactions and payments using **encryption**.

front: Why does internet banking save a customer time and money?
back: It **reduces the need for branch visits**, so there is no travel and no queuing.

front: Give an example of an anti-fraud measure used by an online banking service.
back: **Matching the name of the payee** against the account being paid.

front: Why might a customer still need to visit a bank branch?
back: Because **physical cash cannot be deposited or withdrawn** through internet banking.

front: Why is it easier to make an error with internet banking than in a branch?
back: The customer enters the details themselves, so it is easy to **type in the wrong information**.

front:
**True or False?**

Internet banking can be used without an internet connection.
back:
**False.**

Internet banking **requires a reliable internet connection**.

front: Define **education and training provider**.
back: An education and training provider is responsible for **providing online access to learning resources** for users of all ages.

front: Name the two main features of an education and training provider.
back: **Online support** and **online training courses**.

front: Name the three ways online support can be offered.
back: Through **communication channels**, **knowledge bases** and **additional support resources**.

front: Name three communication channels an education provider might offer.
back: **Email support**, **live chat** and **discussion forums**.

front: Name three things found in a knowledge base.
back: A **frequently asked questions (FAQ) section**, **tutorials and how-to guides**, and **glossaries**.

front: Name three additional support resources an education provider might offer.
back: **Video tutorials**, **webinars** and **downloadable resources**.

front: Name three things an online training course gives learners access to.
back: **Online journals and reference archives**, **online support from teachers and other learners**, and **learning and assessment materials**.

front: Online training courses are often accessed through a virtual learning environment, or <u>**      **</u>.
back: Online training courses are often accessed through a virtual learning environment, or **VLE**.

front: Who are online learning resources aimed at?
back: **Users of all ages**, not only school-age learners.

front: What is the difference between a knowledge base and a communication channel?
back: A **knowledge base** is material the learner reads for themselves, such as FAQs and glossaries, while a **communication channel** connects them to another person, such as email support or live chat.

front:
**True or False?**

Online training courses only provide learning materials, with no support from other people.
back:
**False.**

Online training courses also give **online support from teachers and other learners**.

front: Define **gaming site**.
back: A gaming site is an **online application that hosts a game on a remote server** for users to play, sometimes as a multiplayer game.

front: What are the two purposes of the features a gaming site offers?
back: To **enhance the gameplay** and to **build a community**.

front: What does matchmaking do?
back: It **connects users with other users of a similar skill level**.

front: What do leader boards allow users to do?
back: They allow users to **track progress and compare with others**.

front: Why are cloud saves useful?
back: They **save game progress online**, which ensures **no issues if a user changes devices**.

front: What are microtransactions?
back: **Small in-game purchases** that allow users to **personalise characters** with cosmetics.

front: <u>**        **</u> is downloadable content that offers game expansion.
back: **DLC** is downloadable content that offers game expansion.

front: What is the difference between friends lists and voice chat?
back: **Friends lists and chat** allow users to **connect online**, while **voice chat** allows users to **communicate directly while in the game**.

front: What does livestreaming allow gamers to do?
back: It allows users to **stream their gameplay** so that other users can **watch and interact**.

front: What are esports?
back: **Tournaments hosted on gaming sites** where users **compete for prizes**.

front:
**True or False?**

A gaming site stores the game on the user's own device.
back:
**False.**

A gaming site **hosts the game on a remote server** for users to play.

front: What does a news site give a user?
back: **Up to date access to stories as they break**.

front: How are subscribers alerted to new stories on a news site?
back: Through **notifications**, and a subscriber can **choose what notifications to receive** based on **preferences or categories**.

front: Name four kinds of information besides stories that a news site can provide.
back: **Weather**, **sports**, **stock markets** and **currency values**.

front: Define **auction site**.
back: An auction site allows a user to **list an item for sale and accept bids until a predetermined deadline**.

front: Who wins an online auction?
back: The user with the **highest bid at the deadline**.

front: What does a high buyer rating tell a seller?
back: That the buyer is considered **trustworthy and a fast payer**.

front: What does a high seller rating tell a buyer?
back: That the seller is considered **reliable and posts items promptly**.

front: How can a seller use the rating system to protect themselves?
back: A seller can choose to **only accept bids from buyers with a high rating**.

front: A <u>**                    **</u> price sets a minimum that a seller will accept for an item.
back: A **reserve** price sets a minimum that a seller will accept for an item.

front: What does a 'buy it now' price do?
back: It sets a **price the seller would accept to end the auction early**.

front: Give two things an auction site uses notifications for.
back: To **notify buyers when they are outbid**, and to **remind buyers of auctions that are due to end**.

front:
**True or False?**

On an auction site, only sellers are given a rating.
back:
**False.**

Auction sites use a rating system for **both buyers and sellers**.

front: Define **entertainment provider**.
back: An entertainment provider is an **online platform that provides users with access to digital media**.

front: Name the three ways digital media can be accessed.
back: **On demand**, by **streaming**, and **offline** as downloaded content.

front: What does on demand access allow a user to do?
back: **Browse a library** of movies, TV shows or music and **choose what to watch immediately**.

front: Why does on demand content start playing without a long wait?
back: It **does not require the whole content to be downloaded before playback starts** — content plays **in real time** as long as there is a stable internet connection.

front: What is streaming focused on?
back: **Continuous playback** via **playlists or content with multiple episodes**, selected and played **without downloading**.

front: Offline content is stored on a <u>**            **</u> device, so the internet is not required for playback.
back: Offline content is stored on a **local** device, so the internet is not required for playback.

front: What two forms can a download take?
back: Downloads can be **permanent** or **temporary rented content**.

front: Why do many entertainment platforms offer a mixture of access methods?
back: So that a user has **total flexibility**.

front: Why does streaming music let a user listen on the go?
back: Because **streaming does not require bulky storage** on the device.

front: Why can a user access streamed audio from any device?
back: Because the content is **stored on a server**, not on the device itself.

front:
**True or False?**

A user must download a whole film before they can start watching it on demand.
back:
**False.**

On demand **does not require the whole content to be downloaded before playback starts**; it plays in real time over a stable connection.

front: Name five lifestyle areas positively affected by online goods and services.
back: **Grocery shopping**, **travel booking**, **banking**, **learning** and **information providers**.

front: The availability of online goods and services above all <u>**            **</u> people time.
back: The availability of online goods and services above all **saves** people time.

front: Give three convenience benefits of online grocery shopping.
back: Orders can be placed **at any time from anywhere**, the customer can **choose delivery slots or click and collect**, and there are **no crowds**.

front: Besides convenience, give two benefits of online grocery shopping.
back: **Comparison**, since prices and deals can be compared across different stores in a few clicks, and **variety**, since items are available that local stores may not stock.

front: Give three benefits of booking travel online.
back: It is **time-saving**, since you can find, compare and book all in one place; **flexible**, since bookings are easy to change and last minute deals are available; and gives **choice**, with access to a much bigger variety of options.

front: What does online banking give a user control over?
back: It lets them **track spending and pay bills, all in real time**.

front: Why is online learning described as personalised?
back: **All learning styles are catered for**, and **adaptive platforms adjust to your pace**.

front: Give two other benefits of online learning besides personalisation.
back: It is **accessible**, so you can study anytime, anywhere, and gives **choice**, with access to more subjects and topics than can be found in a traditional classroom.

front: Give two benefits of online information providers.
back: **Speed**, since there is instant access with no waiting, and **variety**, with access to a wide range of information from different viewpoints and perspectives.

front: Name four drawbacks of the availability of online goods and services.
back: Users become **less patient and more demanding**, more **isolated**, more concerned with **checking online communication** at the cost of face-to-face communication skills, and prone to **skim reading** rather than paying attention to detail.

front: How does constant online communication affect a person's social skills?
back: It makes them more concerned with **checking online communication** and **reduces their face-to-face communication skills**.

front: Why does streaming let a user get the latest news?
back: Because a **live recording can be broadcast** as it happens.

front:
**True or False?**

The availability of online goods and services has only positive impacts on lifestyle.
back:
**False.**

It also makes users **less patient and more demanding**, more **isolated**, and more prone to **skim reading** without paying attention to detail.

front: Define **transactional data**.
back: Transactional data is **data that is sent between two connected digital devices** on the internet, and it is **stored in cookies**.

front: Define **cookie**.
back: A cookie is **information left on a user's device** so that a website can **recognise the user when they visit again**.

front: <u>**                    **</u> is used when transmitting cookies.
back: **Encryption** is used when transmitting cookies.

front: Name four kinds of data stored in a cookie.
back: The **time and date of the transaction**, the **IP address**, **data on products or services previously viewed or purchased**, **items added to a shopping cart**, **buttons pressed**, and **data entered into web forms**.

front: Name the three types of cookie.
back: **Session cookies**, **persistent cookies** and **third-party cookies**.

front: What makes a session cookie temporary?
back: It is **lost when you close the browser**, which is why it is considered **less of a privacy concern**.

front: Name three things session cookies are used for.
back: **Keeping track of shopping carts**, **remembering login status** and **form inputs**.

front: How is a persistent cookie different from a session cookie?
back: A persistent cookie is **stored on a local storage device** and has an **expiration date set by the website**, ranging from days to years.

front: Name three things persistent cookies are used for.
back: **Remembering login details for future visits**, **tracking browsing history**, and the **delivery of targeted advertising**.

front: Who owns a third-party cookie?
back: It does **not belong to the website visited** — it is owned by **third parties that provide services to the website**, such as social networking sites and advertising networks.

front:
**True or False?**

Session cookies are a bigger privacy concern than third-party cookies.
back:
**False.**

**Third-party** cookies are the bigger privacy concern because they **create a much larger profile of a user**; session cookies are considered less of a concern because they are lost when the browser closes.

front: Define **targeted marketing**.
back: Targeted marketing is when **third-party cookie data is used to match people** based on their **browsing history or personal attributes**.

front: What determines which adverts a user sees on a site that uses an ad server?
back: The adverts will be **specific to the user's third-party cookie data**.

front: Give two ways transactional data could be used during an online purchase.
back: **Products selected, purchase history or sites visited** could be used to **suggest related products**; **location data** could be used to **set costs**; and **previous preferences or payment details** could **speed up checkout**.

front: What determines whether an online or a local service is better for a user?
back: It depends on the user's **needs and preferences**, weighed across **urgency**, **price**, **choice** and the **online experience**.

front: Give four advantages of online services.
back: **Convenience**, with no travelling and use anytime, anywhere; **selection**, with a wider variety of local, national and international options; **competitive prices**, since online stores have lower costs; and **reviews and ratings** to read before purchasing.

front: Give four disadvantages of online services.
back: **Security** risks from online scams, fraud and data breaches; **returns and exchanges** are inconvenient, especially for bigger items; **delayed gratification** while waiting for items; and **limited customer service** that is impersonal or hard to reach.

front: Why can online stores offer more competitive prices?
back: Online stores typically have **lesser costs**, so they can be very competitive with prices.

front: Give four advantages of local services.
back: **Immediate gratification** with no waiting for deliveries, the ability to **inspect products** before purchasing, **easier returns and exchanges** in person, and **supporting the local economy**.

front: Give four disadvantages of local services.
back: **Limited selection** compared with online, **higher prices** caused by higher overheads, **travel and time** costs, and **limited opening hours**.

front: Local shops charge higher prices because they have higher <u>**                    **</u>.
back: Local shops charge higher prices because they have higher **overheads**.

front: Which type of service suits a customer who needs an item urgently, and why?
back: A **local service**, because it offers **immediate gratification** with **no waiting for deliveries**.

front: Which type of service suits a customer who wants the widest choice, and why?
back: An **online service**, because it gives access to a **wider variety of options** at local, national and international level.

front: Why are returns easier with a local service?
back: Returns and exchanges are **easier in person**, whereas online returns are inconvenient, especially for bigger items.

front: What can a customer do in a local shop that they cannot do online?
back: **Inspect products** and check them before purchasing.

front:
**True or False?**

Online services are always the better choice for a customer.
back:
**False.**

It depends on the user's **needs and preferences** — local services win on **urgency**, **inspecting products**, **returns** and **supporting the local economy**.

front: Define **the cloud**.
back: The cloud describes the **use of the internet to store data and access software**.

front: What is the key difference between accessing data locally and through the cloud?
back: Data and software accessed locally are **confined to the resources of the specific device**, while cloud access **relies on an internet connection**.

front: Define **hosted software**.
back: Hosted software is **software accessed using the internet**, stored on a **remote server** and accessed **through a web browser**.

front: Hosted software can also be called <u>**                    **</u>, or web apps.
back: Hosted software can also be called **web applications**, or web apps.

front: Give four advantages of hosted software.
back: **Access from different types of device**, the ability to **save files online** when combined with online storage, features that **enable collaboration**, **updates and security managed by someone else**, and it is **cost effective** through pay monthly plans.

front: Give four disadvantages of hosted software.
back: It **can only be accessed with an internet connection**, the user experience is affected by **high latency and low bandwidth**, it has **not as many features** as locally installed software, there are **privacy concerns** over who has access to your data, and **hidden fees can add up**.

front: Define **local software**.
back: Local software is software **installed directly onto a device's secondary storage** that **runs from that device without needing an internet connection**.

front: What resources does local software use to run?
back: The **device's own processor, RAM and storage**.

front: How is local software usually paid for, compared with hosted software?
back: Local software is usually purchased with a **one-off licence fee**, while hosted software operates on a **subscription model**.

front: Give three advantages of local software.
back: It **works without an internet connection**, **generally runs faster** using the device's own resources, often includes **more advanced features**, gives the user **full control** over their software and files, and needs **no ongoing subscription**.

front: Give three disadvantages of local software.
back: It **can only be used on the device it is installed on**, has a **higher upfront cost**, the user is **responsible for installing updates** and for **security**, and it **takes up space** on secondary storage.

front: Define **online storage**.
back: Online storage is **long-term secondary storage of data that resides in a remote location**, accessible only **via a wide area network**.

front: Name the three types of online storage.
back: **Public cloud**, where customer and provider are different companies; **private cloud**, where they are a single organisation; and **hybrid cloud**, which combines both.

front: What problem does a hybrid cloud solve?
back: It allows **sensitive data to remain private** while providing **public cloud services for less sensitive information**.

front: Give four advantages of online storage.
back: Data can be **accessed from anywhere and on any device**, it can be **shared with anyone holding permissions**, capacity can be **increased or decreased as needed**, providers use **multiple servers to back data up**, they offer **advanced security features**, and there is **no need to hire specialist staff**.

front: Give four disadvantages of online storage.
back: A **stable internet connection is required**, data may be **vulnerable to security breaches**, the user is **dependent on the provider** for availability and reliability, **all data may be lost if the company ceases to exist**, and the service may become **expensive over time**.

front: Give three advantages of local storage.
back: **No internet connection is needed**, **faster read and write speeds**, the user has **full control over their data and privacy**, it is a **one-off cost**, and it works on **offline devices**.

front:
**True or False?**

Backing up a large music library to cloud storage is quick and free.
back:
**False.**

**Uploads take a long time** because bandwidth is limited and file sizes are large, and there is an **increased cost** since data is often charged per megabyte used.
